## Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One
## In the Majjhima Nikāya
## Commentary on the Mūlapaṇṇāsa (Part Two)
## 3. Opammavagga
## 1. Commentary on the Kakacūpama Sutta

"Thus have I heard" and so forth is the Kakacūpama Sutta. In that sutta, regarding "Moliya-phagguno", "moli" refers to a topknot (crest). As it was said:

"The Great Bodhisatta, the noble among the Sakyans, having cut his topknot scented with excellent perfumes, tossed it into the sky. Sakka, the thousand-eyed lord, holding a precious casket, received it with his head."

That topknot was very large during the lay life of that Venerable Phagguna; therefore, he came to be known as "Moliya-phagguna". Even when he went forth, they knew him by that same name. "Ativelaṃ" means having exceeded the limit (velā). In this context, there are three kinds of limits: the limit of time (kāla-velā), the limit of boundary (sīma-velā), and the limit of virtue (sīla-velā). "At that time (velā), he uttered this inspired utterance" refers to the limit of time. "The established Dhamma does not exceed the limit (velā)" refers to the limit of boundary. "Non-exceeding of the limit is the destruction of the bridge" and "This is called a limit (velā) in the sense of not being transgressed" refer to the limit of virtue. That monk exceeded all three kinds of limits. There is indeed a proper time (kāla) for instructing bhikkhunīs, but that monk, even after the sun had set...
2:
...by instructing them until sunset, he exceeded that *kālavelā*. In the instruction of bhikkhunīs, there is a measure, a boundary, a limit. By instructing beyond five or six words, that Moḷiyaphagguna exceeded that *sīmavelā*. Furthermore, in speaking, by engaging in playful talk that could amount to a *duṭṭhullāpatti* (grave offense), he thus exceeded the *sīlavelā*.

'Saṃsaṭṭho' means being mingled, having shared joys and sorrows. 'Sammukhā' means in the presence of. 'Avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati' means that upon seeing those bhikkhunīs performing tasks such as cooking and pounding [grain], [someone] speaks dispraise, saying, "There is no such thing as non-offense for these bhikkhunīs; these bhikkhunīs are ill-behaved, difficult to admonish, and impudent."

'Adhikaraṇampi karoti' means [the monk] says, "From the time these monks see these bhikkhunīs, their eyes burn; in this monastery, the offering of flowers, the washing of seats, and the plastering work etc. are carried out only by the power of these bhikkhunīs." [The nuns then say,] "These bhikkhunīs are daughters of good family, they are modest; you speak such and such to these bhikkhunīs; such an offense is yours; come to the Vinaya experts and give me a decision," thus dragging them into a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).

'Moḷiyaphaggunassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati' means speaking dispraise, saying, "There is no such thing as non-offense for this monk; the entrance to his cell is never empty of bhikkhunīs." 'Adhikaraṇampi karoanti' means [the nuns] say, "From the time these monks see the Elder Moḷiyaphagguna, their eyes burn; in this monastery, they are not even able to look at the living quarters of others. Bhikkhunīs who come to the monastery receive instruction, greetings, or lessons only by depending on the Elder."

[The monks then say,] "The son of good family is modest and scrupulous; you speak such and such to such a person; come, let the Vinaya experts give a decision," thus dragging them into a legal issue.

'That monk said this to the Blessed One' means he spoke not out of a desire for favor, nor with the intention of causing a schism, but out of a desire for welfare (*atthakāmatā*). It is said he had this thought: "For this monk living thus mingled, ill-repute will arise. That is also a dispraise of the Sasana. If spoken to by another, this monk will not stop; only if the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma and admonishes him will he stop." Thus, out of desire for his welfare, he spoke these words to the Blessed One, beginning with "Venerable Sir, the Venerable..."

'Āmantehi' means "make it known" (call him). 'Āmanteti' means he summons.
3:
"By faith" means through faith (with conviction). "Therefore" (tasmā) is said because you are both a son of a good family and one who has gone forth out of faith; or because displeasure (domanassa) would arise in you—who live in association with those bhikkhunīs—towards those who might abuse or strike you, but such displeasure will not arise when that association is abandoned; hence the word "therefore." In that context, "therein" (tatra) refers to the speaking of that dispraise. "Home-based" (gehasita) means depending on the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Desire" (chanda) refers to both the desire of craving (taṇhā-chanda) and the desire of aversion (paṭigha-chanda). "Perverted" (vipariṇata) means a mind affected by lust is perverted; a mind affected by hatred or delusion is also perverted. However, in this context, it refers to a mind affected by lust through the power of the desire of craving, and a mind affected by hatred through the power of the desire of aversion. "Compassionate for welfare" (hitānukampī) means protecting with a mind associated with welfare, or suffusing with welfare. "Without inner malice" (na dosantaro) means one who will not have a mind of hatred.

Why did the Blessed One begin the teaching starting with "Then the Blessed One..."? It is said that although the monk Moliya Phagguna heard this much instruction, the thought "I will desist and refrain from associating with bhikkhunīs" did not even arise in him. He remained as if in opposition to the Blessed One. Then, just as a hungry person desires food, a thirsty person desires water, a cold person desires heat, and a suffering person desires happiness, the Blessed One, seeing this monk who was difficult to admonish, recalled the monks who were easy to admonish during the first period of Enlightenment (paṭhama-bodhi). Desiring to speak of the virtues of those monks, He began this teaching.

In that context, "they satisfied" (ārādhayiṃsu) means they accepted (the instruction) and fulfilled it. "On one occasion" (ekaṃ samayaṃ) means at a certain time. "Eating in one sitting" (ekāsana-bhojana) means eating a meal only once before noon. Even if one eats seven times from sunrise until noon, it is still intended here as "eating in one sitting." "Freedom from illness" (appābādhatā) means being free from disease. "Freedom from affliction" (appātaṅkatā) means being free from pain. "Lightness of body" (lahuṭṭhāna) means the physical body being light and active. "Strength" (bala) means physical strength. "Living in comfort" (phāsuvihāra) means the physical body dwelling in ease. What is meant by these words? It refers to the time when the afternoon meal (vikāla-bhojana) was caused to be abandoned during the day. In the Bhaddāli Sutta, however, the time when the night meal was caused to be abandoned is mentioned. The Blessed One did not make them abandon both these types of meals at once. Why? Because these two types of meals are habitual for beings in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). There are sons of good families who are delicate; if they were to abandon both meals at once, they would become exhausted. Therefore, instead of making them abandon both at once, He made them abandon the daytime vikāla-bhojana at one time and the nighttime vikāla-bhojana at another time, separately. In this context, it is the time when the daytime vikāla-bhojana was caused to be abandoned...
4:
...is mentioned. In that regard, the Buddhas do not make people abandon (unwholesome things) by showing danger and threatening them; rather, they make them abandon them by showing the benefits (ānisamsa). Only when the benefits are shown in this way can beings abandon them with ease and happiness. Therefore, desiring to show the benefits, He showed these five virtues. "Admonition to be done" (anusāsanī karaṇီyā) means there was no need for repeated admonition in the Dispensation. It was only necessary to prompt mindfulness, saying, "Do this, do not do that." With only that much instruction, those monks performed what was to be done and abandoned what was to be abandoned. "Bhikkhus, in the first period of Enlightenment, the monks were easy to admonish, attentive, and followed the advice."

Now, to illustrate their state of being easy to admonish, He brought forth the simile beginning with "Just as..." (seyyathāpi). In that simile, "on level ground" (subhūmiyaṃ) means on an even surface. (In other texts, however, in the passage "one should plant seeds in good ground, in a good field, where stumps have been removed," the term "subhūmi" refers to fertile soil.) "At a crossroad" (catumahāpathe) means at a place where two great roads intersect and pass through. "A thoroughbred carriage" (ājañña-ratho) is a carriage yoked with well-trained horses. "With the whip laid across" (odhasthapatodo) means having the whip placed crosswise, leaning against the support, so that it can be reached by one standing on the carriage. "A trainer" (yoggācariya) is a horse-trainer. Because he drives horses that are to be tamed, he is called "a charioteer of horses to be tamed" (assadamma-sārathi). "Wherever he wishes" (yenicchakaṃ) means by whatever route he desires. "In whatever way he wishes" (yadicchakaṃ) means in whatever manner of movement he desires. "He might drive forward" (sāreyya) means he would send them straight ahead. "He might drive back" (paccāsāreyya) means he would make them retreat.

"Even so" (evameva kho) means: just as when that trainer wishes to go by a certain route, the horses have already entered that route; and whatever movement he desires, that movement is already achieved. Once the carriage is sent forth, there is no need to restrain or strike the horses; he only needs to watch them go, listening to the sound of the hooves on the level ground. In the same way, for Me, there was no need for repeated speaking to those monks. It was only necessary to prompt mindfulness, saying, "Do this, do not do that." By them, too, at that very moment, what was to be done was already done, and what was not to be done was already abandoned. "Therefore" means: since they were easy to admonish and like a well-yoked vehicle, abandoning (unwholesome states) by a mere prompt to mindfulness, you too should abandon them. "With castor oil plants" (elaṇḍehi) is said because castor oil plants are spoilers of Sāla forests. "He would clear" (visodheyya) means he would clean the forest by cutting down the castor oil plants and other creepers and taking them outside. "Well-grown" (sujātā) means well-established. "He would properly maintain" (sammā parihareyya) means (protecting) from time to time by building embankments and watering.
5:
One should nurture and grow [the tree] well by digging at the main roots, by cutting away creepers and thickets, by removing ant nests, and by clearing away spider webs and dry twigs. The words such as 'growing' have the meanings already stated. 

Now, wishing to show the fault of impatience, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'Bhūtapubbaṃ' (Once upon a time). In that passage, 'Videhikā' refers to the daughter of a wealthy merchant who lived in the kingdom of Videha. Alternatively, wisdom is called 'veda'; because she strives and conducts herself with wisdom, she is called 'Videhikā,' meaning a wise woman. 'Gahapatānī' means the mistress of the house. 'Kittisaddo' means the sound of fame. 'Sorata' means being endowed with gentleness. 'Nivāta' means having a humble manner. 'Upasanta' means being at peace through the subsiding of defilements. 'Dakkha' means being skillful in tasks such as cooking rice, spreading beds, and lighting lamps. 'Analasa' means being energetic; 'Susaṃvihitakammanta' means having well-arranged work. This indicates that while some women may not be lazy, they break whatever vessels they handle or make holes in them; this Videhikā was not that kind of woman.

'Divā uṭṭhāsi' means getting up when the sun is high, without performing the early morning duties such as milking the cows. 'He Je Kāḷī' means calling out, 'Hey, Kāḷī!' 'Kāḷī, why did you get up late?' is a question asking, 'Is there something wrong with you? Why did you get up when the sun is high?' When the maid replied, 'Mistress, there is nothing wrong with me,' Videhikā became angry and displeased, saying, 'Hey, you wretched slave, if there is nothing wrong with you, if your head does not ache and your back does not pain, then why did you get up late?' and she frowned. 'Divātaraṃ uṭṭhāsi' means getting up even later on the following day. 'Displeased speech' refers to her speaking angry words, saying, 'Hey, you wretched slave, do you not know your place? Do you think fire is cold? Now I shall teach you a lesson,' and so forth.

'Paṭivisaka' refers to those living in nearby houses. 'Ujjhāpesi' means causing them to disparage her. 'Caṇḍī' means one who is not gentle, a fierce person. Thus, whatever virtues she had, twice as many faults appeared. Virtues come only gradually, but faults spread in a single day. 'Soratasorata' means one who is exceedingly gentle, reaching a state where it could be asked, 'Is this person a Stream-enterer, a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arahant?' 'Phusanti' means they come into view, touching and striking [the senses].
6:
Then, a monk who stands firm in the practice of patience should be known as 'sorata' (gentle). A person who, because he receives excellent robes and other requisites, performs tasks such as massaging the feet and the back at a single word [is not truly gentle]. 'Alabhamāno' means when he does not receive them as he did before [he no longer performs those tasks]. One who truly honors the Dhamma, treats it with respect, cherishes it in his mind, honors it with the four requisites, and shows humility by being respectful toward the Dhamma alone [is truly gentle].

Having thus shown the fault of impatience, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'Pañcime, bhikkhave' (Monks, there are these five...), wishing to show the five ways of speech by which those who endure do so. Therein, 'kālena' means at the proper and suitable time. 'Bhūtena' means with what is real and existent. 'Saṇhena' means with gentle and smooth speech. 'Atthasañhitena' means with speech connected to the benefit and connected to the reason. 'Akālena' and so forth should be understood as the opposites of those terms. 'Mettacittā' means having a mind of loving-kindness that has arisen. 'Dosantarā' means having a mind of hatred, with anger arisen within. 'Tatra' means in those ways of speech. 'Pharitvā' means having pervaded through reflection.

'Tadārammaṇañca'—how does one make the whole world the object of that [loving-kindness]? By taking the person who spoke using the five ways of speech as the object of the mind of loving-kindness, and then again taking all other remaining beings as the object of that same mind of loving-kindness, one is said to make the whole world the object of that [mind]. Here is the meaning of the words: 'Tadārammaṇañca' means making that the object of the mind of loving-kindness; 'Sabbāvantaṃ' means containing all beings; 'Lokaṃ' means the world of beings; 'Vipulena' means by taking many beings as the object; 'Mahaggatena' means belonging to the exalted sphere; 'Appamāṇena' means well-developed; 'Averena' means free from anger; 'Abyābajjhena' means free from suffering. 'Pharitvā viharissāma' (We shall dwell having pervaded) means that with such a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, we shall dwell having pervaded both that person and the entire world, making them the object of that mind through reflection.

Now, wishing to bring a simile to illustrate that meaning, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'Seyyathāpi' (Just as...). Therein, 'apathaviṃ' means the intention to make the earth 'not-earth.' Therein...
7:
*Tatra* means in those various places. *Vikireyya* means taking up soil with a basket and scattering it like seeds. *Oṭṭhubheyya* means spitting. *Apathaviṃ kareyya* means to ask, "Could I, by making an effort through body and speech, make this earth not-earth?" *Gambhīrā* means being as deep as two hundred and forty thousand yojanas in thickness. *Appameyyā* means being immeasurable in width.

In the phrase *evam eva kho*, the comparison is as follows: The earth should be understood as the mind of loving-kindness (*mettacitta*). The man who comes with a hoe and a basket should be understood as the person who comes with the five ways of speech (*vacanapatha*). Just as that man cannot make the great earth not-earth with his hoe and basket, even so, the person who comes with the five ways of speech will not be able to change the mind (to make it corrupted) of one who dwells in loving-kindness.

In the second parable, *haliddiṃ* refers to any yellow color. *Nīlaṃ* refers to a dark blue/green color like bronze-rust or the color of green leaves. *Arūpī* refers to the formless sky (space). The objection is: Is it not said that the space between two pieces of wood, two trees, two dwellings, or two mountains is 'delimited space-form' (*paricchinna-ākāsa-rūpa*)? Why then is it called 'formless' (*arūpī*) here? It is said so because it is intended to deny its state of being visible. Therefore, it is called *anidassana* (invisible). In that space, it is impossible to paint a picture or to make a painted form appear; hence it is called *arūpī*. *Anidassana* means not coming into the range of the eye-consciousness, which is seeing. In this comparison, the sky is like the mind of loving-kindness. The five kinds of dye, including the brush, are like the five ways of speech. The man who comes with the dyes and the brush is like the person who comes with the five ways of speech. Just as that man cannot make a form appear in the sky with those dyes, even so, the person who comes with the five ways of speech will not be able to change the mind of loving-kindness and make anger appear.

In the third parable, *ādittaṃ* means a burning (torch). *Gambhīrā appameyyā* means that the deep parts of this river Ganges are a quarter-yojana, half-yojana, or even one yojana deep. Its width is similarly vast, and its length is five hundred yojanas. Why is the Ganges said to be deep and immeasurable? Because it is impossible to heat it like water in a pot by such an effort (with a grass torch). While it might be possible to heat a small amount of standing water by some means, such as half an inch or a quarter of an inch deep, this Ganges...
8:
...is impossible; therefore, it is said so. In this comparison, the mind of loving-kindness is like the Ganges, and the person who comes with the five ways of speech is like the man who comes with a grass torch. Just as that man cannot heat the Ganges with a burning grass torch, even so, the person who comes with the five ways of speech will not be able to change the mind of loving-kindness.

In the fourth parable, *biḷārabhastā* means catskin bags. *Sumadditā* means well-kneaded. *Suparimadditā* means well-kneaded all around, inside and out. *Tūlinī* means a bag filled with cotton similar to silk-cotton or creeper-cotton. *Chinnasassara* means having a soft/broken sound of its own. *Chinnabhabbhara* means having a soft/broken sound of various pitches. In this comparison, the mind of loving-kindness is like the catskin bag, and the person who comes with the five ways of speech is like the man who comes with a stick or a potsherd. Just as that man cannot make the catskin bag produce a rattling sound like 'sarasara' or 'bharabhara' with a stick or a potsherd, even so, the person who comes with the five ways of speech will not be able to change the mind of loving-kindness and make it followed by anger.

*Ocarakā* means those who perform menial tasks or low-level work. If any monk or nun should corrupt their mind, they would not be able to endure being cut with a saw. *Na me so tena sāsanakaro* means that by not enduring, he is not a follower of my advice. However, there is no offense (*āpatti*) incurred in this context.

*Aṇuṃ vā thūlaṃ vā* means whether the fault is small or large. *Yaṃ tumhe nādhivāseyyātha* means that which you should not endure. *No hetaṃ bhante* means "Venerable Sir, we do not see any way of speech that should not be endured." "It will be for your long-term welfare and happiness"—thus the Blessed One, setting Arahantship as the pinnacle, concluded the teaching according to the sequence of the discourse.

## 2. Commentary on the Alagaddūpama Sutta

This sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Alagaddūpama Sutta. In that sutta, the phrase 'gaddhe bādhayiṃsu' means they killed vultures, thus they are called 'vulture-killers' (gaddhabādhi). Because there were ancestors in his lineage who were vulture-killers, he is called 'one with vulture-killers in his past' (gaddhabādhipubba). The meaning is one born in a family of vulture-killers, or one descended from a lineage of vulture-killers. They are called 'obstacles' (antarāyika) because they create obstacles to heaven and liberation. These obstacles are of five kinds: Kamma, Kilesa (defilement), Vipāka (resultant), Upavāda (insult), and Āṇāvītikkama (transgression of authority).

Among these five, the five heinous crimes (pañcānantariya kamma) are called Kammantarāyika. Similarly, the act of defiling a nun (bhikkhunīdūsaka kamma) is also called Kammantarāyika. However, that act of defiling a nun only creates an obstacle to liberation (Nibbāna), not to heaven. Fixed wrong views (niyata micchādiṭṭhi) are called Kilesantarāyika. The rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) of eunuchs, animals, and hermaphrodites are called Vipākantarāyika. The act of insulting or disparaging Noble Ones (ariya) is called Upavādantarāyika. These remain obstacles only as long as one has not asked for forgiveness from the Noble Ones; they are not obstacles thereafter. The seven classes of offenses (āpatti) committed intentionally are called Āṇāvītikkamantarāyika. These also remain obstacles only as long as one still claims to be a monk, or has not emerged from the offense, or has not confessed the offense; they are not obstacles thereafter.

Among these obstacles, this monk Ariṭṭha was a learned Dhamma preacher (dhammakathika) and knew the other obstacles. However, because he was not skilled in the Vinaya, he did not know the obstacles arising from the transgression of Vinaya rules. Therefore, having gone into seclusion, he thought: 'These laypeople enjoy the five cords of sensual pleasure and yet become Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners. Monks also see delightful forms cognizable by the eye... pe... touch soft tangible objects cognizable by the body, and use soft rugs and coverings, etc. All this is allowable. Why should only the forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles of women be unallowable? These also are allowable.' Thus, comparing one taste with another, and equating enjoyment with desire and lust to enjoyment without desire and lust, he was like one trying to twist very fine silk thread with coarse hemp ropes, or like one comparing Mount Sineru to a mustard seed. Having given rise to a low, wrong view, he questioned: 'Why did the Blessed One establish the first Pārājika rule with such great effort, as if damming the great ocean? There is no fault in this.' Thus, opposing the Knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), obstructing the Knowledge of Intrepidity (vesārajja-ñāṇa), and throwing stumps and thorns into the Noble Path, he struck at the Conqueror's wheel of authority (āṇācakka) by claiming there is no fault in sexual intercourse. Therefore, he said: 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One...' and so forth.

## 
'Evaṃ byā kho' means 'just like this'. In the passages beginning with 'samanuyuñjanti', the act of asking 'What is your view? State your view' is called 'samanuyuñjanti' (cross-questioning). Establishing a view is called 'samanuggāhanti' (firmly grasping). Asking for the reason, 'For what reason do you say this?' is called 'samanubhāsanti' (pressing for reasons).

In the passages beginning with 'aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā' (like a skeleton), sensual pleasures are like a skeleton because they provide little gratification. They are like a piece of meat because they are common to many. They are like a grass torch because they burn continuously. They are like a pit of glowing coals because they cause great burning. They are like a dream because they appear only for a moment. They are like borrowed goods because they are temporary. They are like a fruit-bearing tree because they cause the destruction of limbs and parts. They are like a slaughterhouse because they are oppressive. They are like a sword stake because they pierce. They are like a snake's head because they are fearful and dangerous. 'Thāmasā' means by the power of wrong view. 'Parāmāsā' means by misapprehending with wrong view. 'Abhinivissa voharati' means speaking or demonstrating while firmly adhering to a view.

'Yato kho te bhikkhū' means 'when those monks'. Regarding the statement, 'Venerable sir, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One...', although this monk Ariṭṭha wanted to say 'No' according to his own desire, he admitted it due to the power of the Buddha. It is said that no one is able to speak double-talk in the presence of the Buddhas.

When the Buddha asked, 'Vain man, to whom do you know me to have taught the Dhamma in such a way?', He meant: 'Among Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, Suddas, laypeople, monks, devas, or humans, to whom do you know me to have taught thus?' The phrase 'Then the Blessed One addressed the monks' is a separate connection (anusandhi). It is said that Ariṭṭha thought: 'The Blessed One calls me a vain man; however, merely being called a vain man does not mean there is no supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Paths and Fruits. For the Blessed One also admonished Upasena Vaṅgantaputta with the words "vain man", saying, "Vain man, you have very quickly turned to gathering a following." That elder, striving and exerting himself later on, realized the six higher powers (abhiññā). I too will exert such energy and produce the Paths and Fruits.' Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show that Ariṭṭha was like a yellow leaf fallen from its bond, incapable of further growth, began this discourse.
11:
Monks, what do you think? Does this monk Ariṭṭha, who holds such a view, opposing the Omniscient Knowledge, obstructing the Knowledge of Fearlessness (Vesārajja-ñāṇa), and striking at the wheel of authority of the Tathāgata, possess even a trace of the warmth of knowledge in this Dhamma-Vinaya? Just as when a great fire is extinguished, there might still be a spark the size of a firefly from which a great fire could be rekindled; likewise, is there even a slight warmth of knowledge (ñāṇusmā) in this person, which, if he were to strive, could produce the paths and fruits? "No, Bhante. How could such warmth of knowledge exist in one who holds such a view?" Thus they spoke, rejecting the possibility of any warmth of knowledge that could serve as a condition for the paths and fruits. The monk Ariṭṭha, being dejected, with shoulders drooping and head downcast, unable to see any insight, sat silently scratching the ground with his big toe, reflecting on his own unworthiness: "Even after obtaining such a teaching that leads to liberation, I am one who does not prosper; I have become one whose conditions for the paths and fruits are severed."

## The phrase 'Paññāyissasi kho' is also a separate connection (anusandhi).

Ariṭṭha thought: "Although the Blessed One says that my supporting condition (upanissaya) for the paths and fruits is severed, the Buddhas teach the Dhamma not only to those with supporting conditions but also to those without them. I will receive good advice from the Teacher and perform merit suitable for myself." Then the Blessed One, wishing to stop his desire for advice, said "Paññāyissasi..." and so on. The meaning is: "You, empty man (moghapurisa), will be known only in hell and such places because of this evil wrong view. There is no more good advice for you from me. I have no need for you; here, I will only question the monks."

## The phrase 'Atha kho bhagavā' is also a separate connection (anusandhi).

In this context, the Blessed One purifies the assembly and excludes the monk Ariṭṭha from the group. This is because someone in the assembly might think: "How could this Ariṭṭha say what the Buddha did not say? Did he say it suddenly as soon as the Buddha started the conversation in the midst of the assembly?" Not only Ariṭṭha but others also might have heard such things. Furthermore, one might think, "As the Teacher rebukes Ariṭṭha, he might rebuke me too," and thus fall into silence upon hearing it.
12:
"They will not do all that," they thought. "I have not spoken it, and there is no word heard by another," thus he purifies the view of the assembly with the words "Monks, you too..." and so on. By purifying the view of the assembly, the monk Ariṭṭha is said to be excluded from the group.

Now, wishing to reveal Ariṭṭha's view, he said "Monks, that monk indeed..." and so on. In that text, among the words "apart from sensual pleasures" and so on: "Monks, that monk who holds the view 'There is no danger for one who indulges in them'—that he, apart from defilement-sensuality (kilesa-kāma) and the perceptions and thoughts associated with defilement-sensuality, having abandoned these things, without these things, would indulge in objective-sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and practice sexual intercourse—this is impossible. Such a cause does not exist; it is impossible and out of the question."

Thus the Blessed One revealed Ariṭṭha's view: "Just as a washerman (rajaka) puts together into one bundle clothes that are fragrant, foul-smelling, old, new, clean, and unclean; in the same way, this monk Ariṭṭha makes everything the same: the use of excellent robes and so on by monks free from desire and lust, the dangerous use with desire and lust by laypeople of unsteady virtue, and the obstructive use with desire and lust by monks of steady virtue." Having revealed Ariṭṭha's view, he now said "Monks, here some people..." and so on, wishing to show the fault of poorly learned scriptures (pariyatti).

In that context, "they learn" means they study and memorize. In the words "Sutta" and so on: the two Vibhaṅgas, Niddesa, Khandhaka, and Parivāra; in the Sutta Nipāta, the Maṅgala Sutta, Ratana Sutta, Nālaka Sutta, and Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta; and any other word of the Tathāgata named 'Sutta' should be known as Sutta. All suttas with verses should be known as Geyya, especially the entire Sagāthā-vagga in the Saṃyutta Nikāya. The entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, suttas without verses, and any other word of the Buddha not included in the other eight limbs should be known as Veyyākaraṇa. The Dhammapada, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and the pure verses in the Sutta Nipāta not named 'Sutta' should be known as Gāthā. The eighty-two suttas connected with verses consisting of joy and knowledge should be known as Udāna. The one hundred and ten suttas proceeding in the manner "Thus it was said by the Blessed One" should be known as Itivuttaka. The five hundred and fifty birth stories beginning with the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka should be known as Jātaka. All those proceeding in the manner "Monks, these four wonderful and marvelous things are in Ānanda..."
13:
Discourses connected with wonderful and marvelous things are to be known as Abbhutadhamma. All discourses such as the Cūḷavedalla Sutta, Mahāvedalla Sutta, Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta, Sakkapañha Sutta, Saṅkhārabhājaniya Sutta, and Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta, which are discourses asked after repeatedly gaining knowledge and satisfaction, are to be known as Vedalla.

"They do not examine the meaning" means they do not see or investigate the true meaning and the meaning of cause and effect. "Unexamined" refers to the meaning for those who do not examine or investigate. "They do not endure scrutiny by wisdom" means they do not appear before wisdom, they do not come into the range of vision; it means they are unable to know that "In this place, virtue, concentration, insight, the path, the fruit, the round of suffering, and the cessation of the round are taught." "They learn only for the sake of criticizing others" means they learn with the intention of gaining the benefit of finding fault in the doctrines of others. "And for the sake of liberating their own doctrine" means they learn for this reason alone: that if others find fault in their own doctrine, they will think, "I will liberate it from that fault in this way."

Those people do not enjoy the benefit for the sake of which noble sons learn the Dhamma—namely, the Path or the Fruit. Those who have a wrong grasp do not enjoy the benefit of that Dhamma. Alternatively, even if they are unable to criticize others' doctrines or liberate their own, they still do not enjoy that benefit.

"Alagaddatthika" means one who desires a poisonous snake. "Gada" is a name for poison; because that snake has sufficient (alaṃ) poison, it is called "alagadda." "Bhoga" refers to the body (handling). "Monks, in this Dispensation, some noble sons learn the Dhamma" means they learn by way of the learning for the sake of crossing over (nittharaṇa-pariyatti). There are three types of learning: alagadda-pariyatti (snake-simile learning), nittharaṇa-pariyatti (learning for crossing over), and bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti (treasurer's learning).

Among these three, if a person learns the Buddha's word thinking, "By learning in this way, I will obtain robes and so on, or they will know me in the midst of the four assemblies," and thus learns for the sake of gain and honor, that person's learning is called alagadda-pariyatti. For one who learns in this (wrong) way, it is even better to be asleep without learning the Buddha's word.

However, if a person learns the Buddha's word and fulfills virtue where virtue is mentioned, establishes a collection of concentration where concentration is mentioned, practices insight where insight is mentioned, and develops the path where the path and fruit are mentioned...
14:
...thinking "I will realize the fruit," that person's learning is called nittharaṇa-pariyatti (learning for the sake of crossing over the round of suffering).

The learning of an Arahant (khīṇāsava), however, is called bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti (treasurer-like learning). For that Arahant, there is no suffering (dukkha-sacca) not fully known, no origin (samudaya-sacca) not abandoned, no path (magga-sacca) not developed, or no cessation (nirodha-sacca) not realized. That Arahant is one who has fully known the aggregates, abandoned the defilements, developed the path, and realized the fruit; therefore, when learning the Buddha's word, they learn only as one who preserves the text, guards the tradition, and protects the lineage. Thus, that Arahant's learning is called bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti.

If a worldling (puthujjana), during times of danger such as famine when scholars cannot stay in one place, learns without being weary by going for alms themselves, thinking, "Let not the very sweet word of the Buddha perish; I will preserve the text, establish the lineage, and guard the tradition," does that person's learning become bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti or not? It does not. Why? Because they are not learning while established in the proper position (of a treasurer/Arahant). The learning of a worldling is either alagaddūpama-pariyatti (snake-simile learning) or nittharaṇa-pariyatti. The learning of the seven types of trainees (sekha) is only nittharaṇa-pariyatti. The learning of an Arahant is only bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti. In this context, however, nittharaṇa-pariyatti is intended.

"They endure scrutiny" means in the places where virtue and so on are mentioned, it appears to their wisdom: "Here virtue is taught, here concentration, here insight, here the path, here the fruit, here the round of suffering, and here the cessation of the round." "They also enjoy the meaning of that Dhamma" means they enjoy the benefit of the Path and Fruit for which they learn. Relying on well-grasped learning, they develop the path and realize the fruit, thereby enjoying the benefit of that Dhamma. Even if they are able to criticize others' doctrines or liberate their own doctrine from blame by taking up the desired points, they still enjoy the benefit.

"It leads to their welfare and happiness for a long time" means it leads to welfare and happiness for a long time for those who fulfill virtue and so on where they are mentioned, for those who criticize others' doctrines according to the Dhamma, for those who remove blame from their own doctrine, and for those who, having reached Arahantship, preach the Dhamma in the midst of the assembly and use the four requisites offered by those inspired by the teaching.
15:
Having thus shown the benefits in the well-learned Word of the Buddha, he now speaks the words beginning with "Tasmā tiha, bhikkhave," wishing to urge [the monks] in that very Word of the Buddha. In that Pali, "tasmā" means: because the poorly learned scriptures (pariyatti), like a poorly grasped snake, lead to harm and suffering for a long time. The well-learned scriptures, like a well-grasped snake, lead to welfare and happiness for a long time. Therefore (tasmā) is the meaning. "Tathā naṃ dhāreyyātha" means: you should remember that meaning in that very way; grasp it with that very meaning. "Ye vā panāssu viyattā bhikkhū" means: if there are other distinguished and wise monks such as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, and Mahākaccāna, those monks should be questioned. But unlike the monk Ariṭṭha, one should not introduce mud or rubbish into my Dispensation.

"Kullūpamaṃ" means the Dhamma that is like a raft. "Nittharaṇatthāya" means for the purpose of crossing over the four floods (ogha). "Udakaṇṇavaṃ" means: if water is deep but not wide, or wide but not deep, that water is not called "aṇṇava" (ocean). Only water that is both deep and wide is called "aṇṇava." Therefore, "mahantaṃ udakaṇṇavaṃ" here means a vast and deep body of water. "Sāsaṅka" refers to a place where the dwelling places, stopping places, sitting places, and lying places of thieves are seen. "Sappaṭibhaya" refers to a place where people are seen killed, plundered, or beaten by thieves. "Uttarasetu" is a bridge constructed over the ocean. Regarding "kullaṃ bandhitvā," a "kulla" (raft) is something bound together as a bundle for the purpose of crossing. Planks, potsherds, etc., spread out and bound together are called "uḷumpa" (a small float). "Uccāretvā" means having set aside. "Kiccakārī" means one who does what should be done, one who does what is appropriate.

In the phrase "dhammāpi vo pahātabbā," "dhamma" refers to serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). The Blessed One causes the abandonment of desire and lust (chandarāga) in both serenity and insight. Where does he cause the abandonment of desire and lust in serenity? "Udāyi... thus I speak of the abandonment even of the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Udāyi... do you see any fetter, small or large, whose abandonment I do not speak of?" In this passage, he causes the abandonment of desire and lust in serenity. "Bhikkhus... if you do not cling to this view which is so pure and bright, if you do not cherish it, if you do not possessively grasp it as 'mine'..." In this passage, [he causes the abandonment of] desire and lust in insight...
16:
...He caused the abandonment [of desire and lust in both tranquility and insight]. In this Dispensation, however, causing the abandonment in both, He said: "You should abandon even dhammas, how much more so non-dhammas (adhamma)." This is the meaning: "Monks, I speak of the abandonment of desire and lust even in such peaceful and sublime dhammas; how much more so in this unrighteous practice (asaddhamma), this village practice (gāmadhamma), this low practice (vasaladhamma), this coarse practice (duṭṭhulla), which ends in the washing with water (odakantika)?" In that practice, this fatuous man Ariṭṭha, perceiving it as faultless, says: "Desire and lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa) are not an obstacle." The Blessed One rebuked Ariṭṭha alone with this instruction, saying: "You should not throw mud or rubbish into my Dispensation as the monk Ariṭṭha did."

Now, wishing to show that whoever grasps the five aggregates as "I" or "mine" through the power of the three types of grasping (craving, conceit, and view) is one who throws mud and rubbish into the Dispensation like this Ariṭṭha, He said: "Monks, these six [bases of views]..." and so on. In that Pali, "basis of views" (diṭṭhiဋ္ဌāna) means: the view itself is a basis of view, the object of the view is a basis of view, and the condition (paccaya) for the view is also a basis of view. 

In the phrases such as "Form is mine" (rūpaṃ etaṃ mama), "This is mine" (etaṃ mama) is grasping through craving (taṇhā). "This I am" (eso hamasmi) is grasping through conceit (māna). "This is my self" (eso me attā) is grasping through view (diṭṭhi). In this way, craving, conceit, and view taking form as their object are spoken of. However, form should not be called "self" (attā). The same method applies to feeling (vedanā) and so on. 

"Seen" (diṭṭha) refers to the base of visible forms (rūpāyatana). "Heard" (suta) refers to the base of sounds (saddāyatana). "Sensed" (muta) refers to the base of smells (gandhāyatana), the base of tastes (rasāyatana), and the base of tangibles (phoṭṭhabbāyatana). Because these [smells, tastes, and tangibles] are grasped by reaching them [with the sense organs], they are called "sensed" (muta). The remaining seven bases (such as the base of mental objects, etc.) are called "cognized" (viññāta). 

"Attained" (patta) is what is obtained whether by seeking or without seeking. "Sought" (pariyesita) is what is sought, whether obtained or not. "Pondered by the mind" (manasānuvicaritaṃ) is what is repeatedly thought about with the mind. In the world, there are things obtained by seeking and things not obtained by seeking. There are things obtained without seeking and things not obtained without seeking. Among these four, what is obtained by seeking is called "attained" (patta). What is not obtained by seeking is called "sought" (pariyesita). Both what is obtained without seeking and what is not obtained without seeking are called "pondered by the mind" (manasānuvicarita). 

Alternatively, what is obtained, whether by seeking or without seeking, is called "attained" (patta) in the sense of being reached. What is not obtained by seeking is called "sought" (pariyesita). What is not obtained without seeking is called "pondered by the mind" (manasānuvicarita). Or, all of these are called "pondered by the mind" because they are repeatedly thought about with the mind. By these [seen, heard, sensed, cognized], craving, conceit, and view taking consciousness as their object are spoken of. Through the elegance of the teaching (desanāvilāsa), consciousness [is explained] by way of the objects such as the seen, etc., below...
17:
(The soul/consciousness) has been shown. "That which is a ground for views" (yampi taṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ) refers to the ground for views that arises in the manner beginning with "That world [is the self]."

"That world is that self" refers to the view arising in the manner beginning with "One regards form as self," which is spoken with reference to taking the world and the self [as permanent]. "I shall be that after death" means "When I have gone to the next world, I shall be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change; I shall remain just so, like the eternal Sineru, the great earth, and the great ocean." "That [view] is also mine" means repeatedly regarding that very [wrong] view as "This view is mine, this I am, this is my self." By this, craving, conceit, and views that take a view as their object are spoken of. This occurs when a later view grasps a preceding view, just as in the case of insight into insight (paṭivipassanā).

On the bright side (sukkapakkha), by the sentence "This form is not mine," the grasping of form through craving, conceit, and views is rejected. The same should be understood for the aggregates beginning with feeling (vedanā). The meaning of the word "samanupassati" (regards/observes) is the four kinds of observation: observation through craving, observation through conceit, observation through views, and observation through knowledge. Among these, on the dark side (kaṇhapakkha), it should be understood by way of the first three observations, and on the bright side (sukkapakkha), by way of observation through knowledge. "He is not anxious about what is non-existent" means that when [the five aggregates] are non-existent, he does not tremble or worry due to fear or craving. With these words, the Blessed One brings the teaching to its climax by showing the Arahant who is not anxious even when the five aggregates within his own continuity are destroyed.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, a certain bhikkhu skilled in connecting the sequence of the teaching thought: "The Blessed One has concluded the teaching by showing the Arahant who is not anxious at the destruction of the internal aggregates. Just as there is one who is not anxious internally, there must also be one who is anxious internally, and one who is anxious or not anxious at the destruction of external requisites. For these four reasons, this question should be asked." Having thought so, he arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his joined palms in salutation, and said this to the Blessed One. "Non-existent externally" refers to the destruction of external requisites. "It was mine, indeed" means "I indeed had a good vehicle, gold, silver, and so on." "That is mine no more" means "That is no longer mine now; it has been taken by kings or thieves, or destroyed by fire or carried away by water."
18:
Or it has worn out through use. "May I indeed have a vehicle, elephants and horses, silver, gold, hill-paddy, grain, barley, or wheat" might be [the wish]. Not obtaining those things, he sorrows: "Because I sat without doing the work appropriate for obtaining those things, I do not have them now." This is the sorrow of a householder (agāriyasocanā). The sorrow of a monk should be understood by way of the bowl, robes, and so forth.

In the section on non-anxiety (aparitassanāvāra), "It does not happen thus" means that because those defilements that would cause such longing have been abandoned, it does not happen in this way. "Grounds for views, standpoints, obsessions, and underlying tendencies of adherence" should be understood by way of views, the preceding views that are the grounds for views, the bases for views, the obsessions that are views, and the adherence and underlying tendencies that think "Only my view is true, the views of others are empty."

"For the stilling of all formations" (sabbasaṅkhārasamathāya) is for the sake of Nibbāna. For, having reached Nibbāna, all the tremblings, stirrings, and fluctuations of all formations are stilled and calmed; therefore, it is called "the stilling of all formations." Only by reaching that Nibbāna are these acquisitions (upadhi) relinquished: the acquisition of the aggregates (khandhūpadhi), the acquisition of defilements (kilesūpadhi), the acquisition of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhārūpadhi), and the acquisition of the five cords of sensual pleasure. Craving is exhausted, fades away, and ceases. Therefore, it is called "the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation." "For Nibbāna" is a designation of its nature. Thus, by all these terms, the purpose of the Blessed One in teaching the Dhamma for the sake of the realization of Nibbāna is shown.

"To him it occurs thus" means that to one with such a view, it occurs: "I shall be annihilated, I shall perish, I shall be no more." When a person with views hears the Dhamma being taught concerning emptiness (suññatā) by applying the three characteristics, anxiety arises. For it has been said: "Bhikkhus, this is anxiety for the uninstructed worldling: 'May I not be! May it not be for me!'"

Thus far, emptiness has been taught in four aspects: one who is anxious and one who is not anxious at the destruction of external requisites, and one who is anxious and one who is not anxious at the destruction of internal aggregates. Now, in order to show emptiness in three aspects by designating external requisites as "possession" (pariggaha), the twenty-fold identity view as "clinging to the doctrine of self" (attavādupādāna), and the sixty-two views headed by identity view as "dependence on views" (diṭṭhinissaya), He said: "Bhikkhus, that possession..." and so on. Therein, "possession" refers to external requisites. "You should possess" means as wise men...
19:
(A wise person) should be able to grasp [this]. He shows: "Monks, you do not see it, nor do I see it; such a grasping (of the doctrine of self) does not exist." In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

Having shown the three-fold emptiness in this way, he now wishes to show the two-fold teaching by taking the internal aggregates as "self" and external requisites as "belonging to self," and thus said: "Monks, when there is a self..." and so on. The summary of the meaning in that Pali text is as follows: Monks, if there were a self, there would be [the thought], "This collection of requisites belongs to my self." Or, if there were requisites belonging to a self, there would be [the thought], "This is my self, the owner of these requisites." Thus, if there is the obsession of "I," it is appropriate that there be the obsession of "mine"; and if there is the obsession of "mine," it is appropriate that there be the obsession of "I." Saccato means truly; thetato means without distortion or firmly.

Now, showing that one who does not grasp these five aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self through these three modes (characteristics) is like the monk Ariṭṭha, who throws mud and rubbish into my Dispensation, he said: "Monks, what do you think? Is form permanent?" and so on. In that passage, "Venerable sir, it is impermanent" means: Venerable sir, it is impermanent because it does not exist after having come to be. Or, it is impermanent for four reasons: because it follows the process of arising and passing away, because it is of a changing nature, because it is temporary, and because it rejects permanence. "Venerable sir, it is suffering" means: Venerable sir, it is suffering in the sense of being oppressive. Or, it is suffering for four reasons: because of the suffering of burning, because it is the basis of suffering, because it rejects pleasure, [and the sense of oppression]. "Of a changing nature" means having the nature of passing into another existence, or having the nature of abandoning its original state. "Is it fit to regard that as: This is mine, this I am, this is my self?" means: Is it fit to grasp it as "I" and "mine" through the power of these three graspings—craving, conceit, and wrong view? By the words "No, venerable sir," those monks acknowledge that "Venerable sir, form is non-self" by way of its being uncontrollable. Or, it is non-self for four reasons: because it is void, ownerless, not under control, and because it rejects a self.

The Blessed One shows the state of non-self through the power of impermanence (anicca) in some places, through the power of suffering (dukkha) in some places, and through the power of both in some places. "If anyone should say, 'The eye is self,' that is not tenable. The arising and passing away of the eye are evident. Since arising and passing away are evident, if one were to say 'The eye is self,' it would follow that 'My self arises and passes away.' Therefore, it is not tenable to say 'The eye is self.' Thus, the eye is non-self." In this Chachakka Sutta, he shows the state of non-self through the power of impermanence. "And this form..."
20:
"Monks, if form were self, this form would not lead to affliction, and it would be possible to say of form: 'Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.' But because, monks, form is non-self, form leads to affliction, and it is not possible to say of form: 'Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.'" In this Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta, he shows the state of non-self through the power of suffering. "Monks, form is impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self; what is non-self should be seen as it actually is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'" In this Arahatta Sutta, he shows the state of non-self through the power of both [impermanence and suffering]. Why? Because impermanence and suffering are evident, but non-self is not evident.

Indeed, when vessels and such things used [in daily life] break, people say, "Alas, it is impermanent!" (Aho aniccaṃ), but there is no one who says, "Alas, it is non-self!" (Aho anattā). When boils, carbuncles, or sores arise on the body, or when one is pierced by a thorn, people say, "Alas, it is painful!" (Aho dukkhaṃ), but there is no one who says, "Alas, it is non-self!" (Aho anattā). Why? Because this characteristic of non-self is not manifest, is difficult to see, and difficult to make known. Therefore, the Blessed One shows that non-self through the power of impermanence, or through the power of suffering, or through the power of both. This [non-self] is shown in this [sutta] as well through the power of impermanence and suffering in three modes. The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates.

"Therefore, monks" (tasmā tiha) means: Monks, because form is impermanent, suffering, and non-self now as well as at other times. The terms "Whatever form" (yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ) and so on have been explained in detail in the Khandha-niddesa of the Visuddhimagga.

"He becomes disenchanted" (nibbindati) means he becomes weary. Here, by "disenchantment" (nibbidā), "insight leading to emergence" (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) is intended. Insight leading to emergence has many names. In some places, it is called "the peak of perception" (saññagga). In some places, "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa). In some places, "factor of the effort for purification" (pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅga). In some places, "purification by knowledge and vision of the way" (paṭipadāṇāṇadassanavisuddhi). In some places, "the exhaustion of identification" (tammayatāpariyādāna). In some places, it is called by three names, and in some places by two.

Among those, in the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta, it is called "the peak of perception" thus: "Poṭṭhapāda, first perception arises, then knowledge." In the Susima Sutta, it says: "Susima, first..."
21:
In the Saṃyutta Nikāya, it is taught under the name of Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa (knowledge of the stability of Dhamma) as: "First, the knowledge of the stability of Dhamma arises; afterwards, the knowledge of Nibbāna." In the Dasuttara Sutta, it is taught as Pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅga (factor of striving for purification) as: "The factor of striving for the purification of knowledge and vision of the way." In the Rathavinīta Sutta, it is taught under the name of Paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi (purification of knowledge and vision of the way) as: "Friend, is the holy life lived under the Blessed One for the sake of the purification of knowledge and vision of the way?" In the Saḷāyatana Vibhaṅga, it is taught under the name of Tammayatāpariyādāna (the exhaustion of involvement) as: "Monks, depending on atammayatā (non-involvement), relying on atammayatā, there is that equanimity based on diversity, supported by diversity; avoiding that, there is that equanimity based on unity, supported by unity; depending on that, relying on that, thus there is the abandoning of this equanimity, thus there is the transcending of this equanimity." In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it is taught by three names: "The knowledge of the desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatāñāṇa), the knowledge of reflective contemplation (paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇa), and the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa) are one in meaning and differ only in phrasing." In the Paṭṭhāna, it is taught by two names: "Conformity (anuloma) assists change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) by way of proximity condition (anantarapaccaya); conformity assists purification (vodāna) by way of proximity condition." In this Alagaddūpama Sutta, however, it appears under the name of nibbidā (disenchantment) as "he becomes disenchanted."

In the phrase "being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate," virāga (dispassion) refers to the Path (magga). In the phrase "through dispassion, he is liberated," the Fruit (phala) is taught as liberation through the Path of dispassion. In the phrase "when liberated, there is the knowledge that he is liberated," the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa) is taught.

Having thus shown the great khīṇāsava (one whose taints are exhausted) with a liberated mind, the Buddha now, wishing to express the name of that Arahant through five factual reasons, said: "Monks, this monk is called (one who has lifted the bolt)," and so on. Avijjā (ignorance) is the ignorance that is the root of the round of rebirths. This ignorance is called a "bolt" (paligha) because it is difficult to remove. Because that bolt of ignorance has been lifted, that Arahant is called "one who has lifted the bolt" (ukkhittapaligha). "Made like a palm-tree stump" (tālāvatthukatā) means made like a palm tree with its head cut off, or like the site where a palm tree stood after being uprooted along with its roots. Just as that palm tree is no longer seen at that site, it means it has been brought to a state of non-existence again. "Ponobbhavika" refers to (craving) that gives rise to renewed existence. In the words "the round of births" (jātisamsāra) etc., the cause of the aggregates of renewed existence, so named by way of being born (jāyana) and by way of wandering (saṃsaraṇa), is the volitional formations of kamma (kammābhisaṅkhāra). Because that kammābhisaṅkhāra stands surrounding [the being] by way of repeatedly causing rebirth, it is called a "moat" (parikkhā); because that moat has been destroyed...
22:
...it is called parikkhā. Taṇhā (craving) is the craving that is the root of the round of rebirths. This craving is called a "pillar" (esikā) because of its deep-seated nature. Because that pillar of craving has been pulled up and discarded, that noble person is called "one who has pulled up the pillar" (abbuḷhesika).

Orambhāgiya refers to the (fetters) that are the causes of rebirth in the sense-sphere. Because these fetters stand blocking the mind like a door-leaf blocks a city gate, they are called "latches" (aggaḷa). Because those latches have been abandoned and broken, that person is called "one who is unlatched" (niraggaḷa).

Ariya (noble) means one who is free from defilements and is pure. Pannaddhaja (one who has lowered the banner) means one who has lowered the banner of pride (māna). Pannabhāra (one who has laid down the burden) means one who has laid down the burden of the aggregates, the burden of defilements, the burden of volitional formations, and the burden of the five cords of sensual pleasure. However, in this context, pannabhāra is intended as one who has laid down the burden of pride. Visamyutta (detached) means one who is detached from the four yokes and all defilements. But here, visamyutta is intended as being detached from the yoke of pride. Asmimāna (the "I am" conceit) is the conceit "I am" in regard to form, the conceit "I am" in regard to feeling... perception... formations... and consciousness.

By this much, the Blessed One has shown the time of the Arahant (khīṇāsava) who, having exhausted the defilements through the Path, has reached the noble bed of cessation (nirodha) and dwells having attained the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) with Nibbāna as the object. For example, suppose there are two cities: one is a city of thieves (coranagara) and one is a safe city (khemanagara). Then a great warrior might think: "As long as this city of thieves exists, the safe city cannot be free from danger; I will make the city of thieves a non-city (destroy it)." Having put on full armor and taken a sword, he approaches the city of thieves, cuts down the pillars (esikā) erected at the city gate with his sword, cuts the door-leaf along with the door-posts, removes the bolt (paligha), breaks the wall, fills the moat (parikkhā), lowers the banners (dhaja) raised for the city's beauty, burns the city with fire, enters the safe city, ascends the palace, and surrounded by his relatives, eats excellent food. In the same way, the city of thieves is like the sakkāya (the five aggregates), the safe city is like Nibbāna, and the great warrior is like the practitioner (yogāvacara). That person thinks: "As long as the round of sakkāya continues, there is no escape from the 32 kinds of torture, the 98 kinds of diseases, and the 25 kinds of great dangers." Like that great warrior, he puts on the armor of virtue (sīla), takes the sword of wisdom (paññā), and just as the warrior cuts the pillars with his sword, he pulls up the pillar of craving with the Path of Arahantship; just as that warrior cuts the city gate with its door-posts, he opens the latch of the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana); just as that warrior removes the bolt, he removes the bolt of ignorance (avijjā); and just as that warrior breaks the wall and fills the moat...
23:
That hero, destroying the karmic formations (kammābhisaṅkhāra) and filling the moat of the round of rebirths (jātisaṃsāra), lowering the banners of conceit (māna) like banners raised for the beauty of a city, and burning the city of identity (sakkāya), enters the city of Nibbāna—the cooling of defilements—like a hero eating excellent food in a palace in a safe city, and spends his time experiencing the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) with the deathless cessation (amatanirodha) as the object.

Now, wishing to show that the consciousness of an Arahant whose mind is thus liberated cannot be known by others, he said the words beginning with "Vimuttacittaṃ kho." In that context, "anvesanti" means searching. "Idaṃ nissitaṃ" means it is dependent on such and such an object. In this term "Tathāgatassa," it refers to a being as a Tathāgata, and also to the supreme person, the Arahant (khīṇāsava). "Anannuvijjo" means not being manifest or not being found. If the term Tathāgata is taken as a being, the meaning "not being manifest" is appropriate; if it is taken as an Arahant, the meaning "not being found" is appropriate.

Between those two, the meaning in the first method is: Monks, I do not designate the Arahant who is still living in this very life as a "Tathāgata, a being, or a person." How then could I designate an Arahant who has attained Parinibbāna and has no further rebirth as a "being" or a "person"? A Tathāgata is one who cannot be found. In truth, in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a being; how then could those who search for the consciousness of that non-existent being find it, saying, "This consciousness is dependent on this object"? How could they obtain it?

In the second method, the meaning is: Monks, I say that even an Arahant living in this very life cannot be found through his consciousness by Indra and others. Indeed, even the devas and brahmas, including Indra, Brahma, and Pajāpati, though they search, are not able to know the insight-consciousness, the path-consciousness, or the fruition-consciousness of an Arahant, thinking, "It occurs dependent on such and such an object." How then could they know the Arahant who has attained Parinibbāna and has no further rebirth?

"Asatā" means by what is non-existent. "Tucchā" means by what is vain. "Musā" means by a false statement. "Abhūtena" means by what is not true. "Abbhācikkhanti" means they accuse or speak by way of oppression. "Venayiko": because he destroys, it is called 'vinaya'; that very 'vinaya' is called 'venayika,' meaning one who destroys beings. "Yathā cāhaṃ na bhikkhave" means: Monks, in which manner I am not a destroyer of beings. "Yathā cāhaṃ na vadāmīti" means: for which reason I do not [declare] the destruction of beings...
24:
I declare. The meaning is: Just as I am not a destroyer of beings, and just as I do not declare the destruction of beings, yet those venerable ascetics and brahmins, saying, "The ascetic Gotama is an annihilator (venayika)," meaning the ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of beings, and saying, "He declares the cutting off, the destruction, and the non-existence of an existing being," meaning he declares the destruction of beings—they accuse me with what is non-existent, vain, false, and untrue.

"Pubbe ca" means formerly, at the very site of the Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa). "Etarahi ca" means and now, at the time of teaching the Dhamma. "Dukkhañceva paññapemi, dukkhassa ca nirodhaṃ" means that whether while residing at the site of Enlightenment before preaching the Dhammacakka, or while teaching the Dhamma from the time of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma onwards, he declares only the Four Noble Truths. Here, it should be understood that by the word 'dukkha' (suffering), its root cause, the Truth of Origin (samudaya), is also taken; and by the word 'nirodha' (cessation), the Truth of the Path (magga) which leads to that cessation is also taken.

"Tatra ca" means in that manifestation of the Four Noble Truths. "Pare" refers to persons who are unable to know or penetrate the Truths. "Akkosanti" means they insult with the ten grounds for insults. "Paribhāsanti" means they abuse with words. "Rosenti vihesenti" means they annoy and harass with the intention to trouble and harm. "Tatra" means in those insults and so on, or towards those other persons. "Āghāto" means anger. "Appaccayo" means displeasure. "Anabhiraddhi" means dissatisfaction.

"Tatra ca" means in that very manifestation of the Four Noble Truths. "Pare" refers to persons who are able to know and penetrate the manifestation of the Four Noble Truths. "Ānando" means the rapture of joy. "Uppilāvitattaṃ" means the rapture of elation.

"Tatra ca" means in that very manifestation of the Four Noble Truths. "Tatra" means in the offerings and honors (sakkāra) and so on. "Yaṃ kho idaṃ pubbe pariññātaṃ" means these five aggregates were previously fully understood at the site of Enlightenment through the three types of full understanding (pariññā). "Tatthame" means these [honors] occur in those five aggregates. What is meant? Even when such offerings and honors are made, it does not occur to the Tathāgata that "These honors are being done to me" or "I am enjoying these honors." It is only that the five aggregates, which were previously fully understood, enjoy these honors; it is only this much. "Tasmā" means because those who are unable to penetrate the Truths insult even the Tathāgata, therefore [it is so]. The rest should be understood in the same manner as already stated.
25:
Monks, therefore, abandon what does not belong to you. Abandoning desire and lust even for the self, which is not one's own, will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. This means: therefore, abandon the five aggregates which do not belong to you. The phrase 'may do as they please' means that in whatever manner they wish to act, they can act in that manner. The monks replied, 'Venerable Sir, these grasses, wood, branches, and leaves are not our self, nor are they our form or consciousness.' The phrase 'not one's own' means it is not even our requisites such as robes. Monks, in the same way, when the Blessed One said, 'Abandon what is not yours,' He was showing that only the five aggregates are not yours and was causing them to be abandoned. In causing them to be abandoned, He did not do so by means of uprooting or tearing away (the body), but rather by the removal of desire and lust (chandarāga).

In the phrase 'thus well-expounded,' this should be brought in from the discourse of the three-fold rotation (tiparivaṭṭa) up to this point, and also from the discourse on the destination of heaven through mere affection in reverse order (paṭiloma) up to this point. 'Svākkhāta' means well-spoken. Because it is well-spoken, it is clear, open, and revealed. 'Chinnapilotika': pilotikā refers to old cloth that is cut, broken, sewn here and there, knotted, and worn out; one who does not have such rags but wears a brand new cloth of eight or nine cubits is called 'chinnapilotika' (one free from rags). This Dhamma is also like that; in this Dhamma, there is no state of being cut, broken, sewn, or knotted by way of deceit (kuhana) and so forth. Alternatively, rubbish is also called 'pilotika.' In this Dispensation (Sāsana), what is called 'ascetic-rubbish' (samaṇakacavara) finds no footing. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Drive out the rubbish-monk, remove the refuse,
Sweep away the chaff, those who are non-ascetics but think themselves ascetics.
Having driven out those of evil desires and evil conduct,
You who are pure, dwell together with the pure, being mindful.
Then, being united and wise, you shall make an end of suffering.' (Sn. 283-285)

Because the ascetic-rubbish has been cut off and removed, this Dhamma is also called 'chinnapilotika.' 'There is no round (vaṭṭa) for them to be designated' means their round of rebirth has reached a state of non-designation (is nameless). Such a great Arahant appears only in a well-expounded Dispensation like this. Just as it is for the Arahant, so it is for the Non-returner (Anāgāmī) and others.
26:
In that context, the 'Dhamma-follower' (dhammānusārī) and the 'Faith-follower' (saddhānusārī) are these two types of persons standing on the Path of Stream-entry. As it was said: "What kind of person is a Dhamma-follower? For a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry, the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) is predominant; he develops the Noble Path led by wisdom, conveyed by wisdom. This person is called a Dhamma-follower. A person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry is a Dhamma-follower; when standing in the fruit, he is 'one attained to vision' (diṭṭhippatta). What kind of person is a Faith-follower? For a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is predominant; he develops the Noble Path led by faith, conveyed by faith. This person is called a Faith-follower. A person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry is a Faith-follower; when standing in the fruit, he is 'one liberated by faith' (saddhāvimutta)." (Pug. 30).

By the words "those who have mere faith and mere love for Me," it refers to those who do not possess other noble qualities (ariya-dhamma) but have only mere faith and mere love for the Tathāgata. They should be understood as insight practitioners (vipassaka). For insight-practicing monks who sit having established insight, a unique faith and a unique love for the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala) arises. By that faith and love, it is as if they are taken by the hand and placed in heaven; for it is said their destination (gati) is certain. The ancient Elders, however, call such a monk a 'Lesser Stream-enterer' (cūḷasotāpanna). The remaining meanings are clear in all places.

## The Commentary on the Alagaddūpama Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, is finished.

## 3. Vammikasutta-vaṇṇanā
"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Vammika Sutta. Therein, 'Āyasmā' is a term of endearment. 'Kumārakassapa' is the name of that Elder. Because he ordained while still a youth (kumāra), when the Blessed One said, "Call Kassapa," or "Give this fruit or food to Kassapa," and people asked "Which Kassapa?", the reply was "Kumārakassapa." Having received the name in this way, he was called "Kumārakassapa" even in his old age. Furthermore, because he was the foster son of the King, they knew him as "Kumārakassapa." This is the account of his manifestation starting from his past practice:
27:
That Elder, it is said, was a merchant's son in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. One day, seeing the Blessed One appointing a certain disciple who was an eloquent speaker (citrakathī) to a pre-eminent position, he gave alms to the Blessed One for seven days and made a wish: "Venerable Sir, may I also become an eloquent disciple of a future Buddha, just like this Elder." While performing meritorious deeds, he ordained in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, but was unable to attain any special distinction (magga-phala).

At that time, while the dispensation of the Blessed One who had attained Parinibbāna was declining, five monks bound a ladder, climbed a mountain, and practiced the Dhamma of a recluse. The Senior Elder (Saṅghatthera) attained Arahantship on the third day. The second Elder became a Non-returner (Anāgāmī) on the fourth day. The remaining three monks, unable to attain any special distinction, were reborn in the celestial realm. While enjoying prosperity in the celestial and human realms during the interval between two Buddhas, one was reborn into a royal family in the city of Takkasilā and became a king named Pukkusāti. Having ordained in dedication to the Blessed One, while traveling to Rājagaha, he heard the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching in a potter's shed and attained the Fruit of Non-returning.

Another was reborn in a family home at a seaport. While traveling by ship, the ship was wrecked; he wore bark garments and, having received gains and honors, thought, "I am an Arahant." Urged by a well-wishing deity who said, "You are not an Arahant; go and ask the Teacher a question," he did so and attained the Fruit of Arahantship.

Another was conceived in the womb of a young woman of a noble family in Rājagaha. That woman first pleaded with her parents but did not receive permission to ordain, so she went to her husband's house. Not knowing she was pregnant, she served her husband, and with his permission, she ordained among the bhikkhunīs. Seeing the signs of her pregnancy, the bhikkhunīs questioned Devadatta, who said, "She is not a true nun." They then questioned the Blessed One, and the Teacher assigned the responsibility to Ven. Upāli Thera. The Thera summoned the families living in Sāvatthī and the laywoman Visākhā to investigate. He declared, "The pregnancy occurred before she became a nun; her ordination is faultless." The Teacher gave his approval to the Thera, saying, "The case has been well-decided." That bhikkhunī gave birth to a son who resembled a golden image. King Pasenadi of Kosala took the young boy and had him raised. Naming him "Kassapa," later...
28:
## 
(The King) decorated him and brought him to the Teacher to be ordained. Thus, because he was the foster son of the King, that Elder was known as "Kumāra Kassapa."

Andhavana is the name of the forest where this occurred. That forest is known as "Andhavana" without any change of name during the times of two Buddhas. The explanation of the designation "Andhavana" is as follows: The bodily relics (sarīradhātu) of Buddhas who appear in times of short lifespans do not remain as a single solid mass. By the power of their resolution, they are dispersed. For this reason, our Blessed One also resolved at the time of his Parinibbāna: "I will not remain for a long time; I have been seen by only a few beings. Those who have not seen me are far more numerous. May they take my relics, worship them in various places, and be headed for heaven." He resolved, "May my body be dispersed." However, the bodily relics of Buddhas who appear in times of long lifespans remain as a single solid mass, like a block of gold.

The relics of the Blessed One Kassapa likewise remained as a single solid mass. Thereafter, the people assembled and consulted, "The relics are a single mass and cannot be divided; what shall we do?" They decided, "We shall build a solid stupa (cetiya). How large should it be?" Some said, "Let it be seven yojanas in size." "This size is too large; it will be difficult to maintain in the future. Let it be six yojanas, five yojanas... four yojanas... three yojanas... two yojanas... let it be one yojana," they concluded. Then they discussed, "What should the bricks be like?" They decided, "Let the outer bricks be solid bricks made of red gold (rattasuvaṇṇa), worth a hundred thousand each. Let the inner bricks be worth fifty thousand each. Let the clay-work be done with orpiment (haritāla) and realgar (manosilā), and the water-work be done with oil." Having reached this conclusion, they divided the four entrances into four portions. The King took one entrance; Prince Pathavindara took one; the General, as the head of the ministers, took one; and the Merchant (Setthi), as the head of the country folk, took one.

Among those entrances, because of his wealth, the King had gold brought out and began the work on the entrance he had taken. The Viceroy and the General also began. However, the work on the entrance taken by the Merchant was lagging. Then, a lay follower named Yasorata, who was a bearer of the Tipitaka and an Anāgāmī noble disciple, realized the work was lagging, prepared five hundred carts, and went to the countryside...
29:
Kassapa Buddha, having remained for twenty thousand years, attained parinibbāna. For that Blessed One, a jewel stupa one yojana in size was to be built. An exhortation was made: "Whoever is able to strive to offer gold, silver, the seven kinds of jewels, yellow orpiment, or red arsenic, let that person offer those items." People offered gold, silver, and so forth according to their ability. Those who were unable offered oil, rice, and such. The lay devotee (upāsaka) sent the oil, rice, and other items as provisions and wages for the workers; with the remaining items, he purchased gold and sent it. In this manner, he traveled throughout the entire Jambudīpa.

When the construction of the stupa reached completion, a message was sent from the site of the stupa: "The work is finished; let the teacher come and worship the stupa." That lay devotee also sent a reply: "I have exhorted the people throughout the entire Jambudīpa; take whatever materials there are and complete the work." Both letters met midway on the road. However, the letter from the stupa site reached the teacher's hand before the teacher's own letter reached its destination. After reading the letter, the teacher set out alone, thinking, "I shall worship the stupa."

In a forest along the way, five hundred bandits appeared. Among those bandits, some, upon seeing him, told the others, "This man has collected gold and silver from the entire Jambudīpa; a great pot of treasure has come rolling to us," and they captured him. He asked, "Friends, why do you capture me?" They replied, "You have collected all the gold and silver from the entire Jambudīpa; give some to us as well." He said, "Do you not know? Kassapa Buddha has attained parinibbāna. A jewel stupa one yojana in size is being built for that Blessed One. I have made these exhortations only for that stupa, not for my own benefit. All the materials obtained have been sent to the stupa site from wherever they were received. As for me, apart from the single garment I am wearing, I do not possess even a single farthing of other property."

Some bandits said, "If this is the case, let this teacher go." Others, however, said, "This man is one honored by kings and ministers.
