If he sees any of us in the city streets, he will report us to the king and his great ministers, and bring us to ruin and destruction." The lay devotee said, "Friends, I will not do such a thing." He said this out of compassion for those bandits, not out of a desire for his own life. Then, as the bandits argued whether he should be captured and killed or released, those who held the view that he should be killed became the majority, and thus they deprived the lay devotee of his life.
30:
Due to the offense committed against a noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) endowed with great virtues, the eyes of those bandits vanished like the flame of an extinguished lamp. Crying out, "O friends, where are my eyes? O friends, where are my eyes?", some were taken home by their relatives. Others, being without relatives and helpless, lived in leaf huts at the foot of trees within that very forest. People coming to the forest, out of compassion, gave them rice, food parcels, or provisions. When people who went for wood or leaves were asked, "Where are you going?", they would say, "We are going to Andhavana (Blind Men's Grove)." Thus, during the time of the two Buddhas, that forest became known as "Andhavana."

During the time of Kassapa Buddha, it was a forest in an abandoned district. During the time of our Blessed One, it was a meditation hall (padhānaghara), a dwelling place for sons of good family desiring seclusion, located not far from Sāvatthī, behind the Jetavana monastery. At that time, the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa was residing there, fulfilling the practice of one in higher training (sekha-paṭipadā). Therefore, it is said, "He was residing in Andhavana."

"Aññatarā devatā" means a certain deity who is not prominent by name or clan. In the passage, "Venerable Sir, does the Blessed One know that he once spoke on the liberation through the destruction of craving in brief to a certain (aññatara) eminent deity?", even the well-known Sakka, king of gods, is referred to as "aññatara." The word "devatā" is a general term used for both gods (devaputta) and goddesses (devadhītā), but in this context, it refers to a god.

In the phrase "abhikkantāya rattiyā," the word "abhikkanta" is found in the senses of exhaustion (khaya), excellence (sundara), beauty (abhirūpa), and appreciation (abbhanumodana). Among these, in passages such as, "Venerable Sir, the night has passed (abhikkantā), the first watch has ended, the community of monks has been sitting for a long time; Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the monks," it is found in the sense of exhaustion (khaya). In passages such as, "Among these four persons, this one is more excellent (abhikkantatara) and more sublime," it is found in the sense of excellence (sundara).

"Who is it that worships my feet,
Glowing with psychic power and glory,
Illuminating all directions
With a most beautiful (abhikkanta) complexion?"

In such passages, it is found in the sense of beauty (abhirūpa). In passages such as, "Excellent (abhikkantaṃ), Master Gotama!", it is found in the sense of appreciation (abbhanumodana). In this context, however, it is used in the sense of exhaustion (khaya). Therefore, "abhikkantāya rattiyā" means "when the night had passed." At that time, that deity, at the end of the middle watch...
31:
(It should be understood that the deity) arrived (immediately after the middle watch). In the word "Abhikkantavaṇṇā," the word "abhikkanta" is used here in the sense of being very beautiful. The word "vaṇṇa," however, is found in the senses of skin (complexion), praise, caste (class), cause, form (shape), measure, and visual object (rūpāyatana), etc.

Among those meanings, in sentences such as "The Blessed One is of golden complexion," it is used in the sense of skin (complexion). In sentences such as "Householder Upāli, when did you compose these praises of the ascetic Gotama?" it is used in the sense of praise. In sentences such as "O Gotama, there are these four castes," it is used in the sense of caste. In sentences such as "For what reason am I called a thief of fragrance?" it is used in the sense of cause. In sentences such as "Having created the form of a great elephant king," it is used in the sense of form. In sentences such as "There are three measures for an alms-bowl," it is used in the sense of measure. In sentences such as "Color, smell, taste, and nutritive essence," it is used in the sense of visual object. Here, however, the word "vaṇṇa" should be understood in the sense of skin (complexion). Therefore, "Abhikkantavaṇṇā" means having a very beautiful complexion, a desirable complexion, a pleasing complexion.

Indeed, when deities come to the human world, they discard their natural appearance and natural power, assume a grosser physical form, and create a superior appearance and power, arriving with a fashioned body like humans going to a festival or performance. This young deity also arrived in the same manner. Therefore, it is said "Abhikkantavaṇṇā."

In the term "Kevalakappaṃ," the word "kevala" has many meanings such as without remainder, mostly, unmixed, not exceeding, firmness, and disconnection (from defilements). Indeed, in sentences such as "The holy life that is entirely complete and pure," it is used in the sense of without remainder. In sentences such as "Most of the people of Aṅga and Magadha will approach taking many kinds of food," it is used in the sense of mostly. In sentences such as "There is the arising of this entire mass of suffering," it is used in the sense of being unmixed. In sentences such as "This venerable one surely has only faith," it is used in the sense of not exceeding. In sentences such as "A co-resident of the Venerable Anuruddha named Bāhiya stands firmly for the sake of schism in the Saṅgha," it is used in the sense of firmness. In sentences such as "He is called a 'Kevalī' (one who is disconnected), one who has lived the life, a supreme person," it is used in the sense of disconnection. Here, however, the meaning of "without remainder" is intended for the word "kevala."

This word "kappa" has many meanings such as belief, usage, time, designation, cutting, conception (alternative), pretext (hint), and entirety. Indeed, "This is to be believed..."
32:
"...by the Venerable Gotama, just as by the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One," in such sentences (the word kappa) is used in the sense of belief. "Bhikkhus, I allow you to enjoy fruit through the five usages of ascetics," in such sentences it is used in the sense of usage (vohāra). "By which I dwell constantly (niccakappaṃ)," in such sentences it is used in the sense of time. "The Venerable Kappa is thus," in such sentences it is used in the sense of designation. "Adorned, with hair and beard trimmed (kappita)," in such sentences it is used in the sense of cutting (chedana). "The two-finger-breadth alternative (dvangulakappa) is allowable," in such sentences it is used in the sense of conception (vikappa). "There is a pretext (lesa) for lying down," in such sentences it is used in the sense of pretext. "Having illuminated the entire (kevalakappaṃ) Veḷuvana," in such sentences it is used in the sense of entirety (samantabhāva). Here, however, the meaning of entirety is intended. Therefore, in the phrase "kevalakappaṃ andhavanaṃ," the meaning should be understood as the entire Andhavana without remainder.

"Obhāsetvā" means having spread the radiance arising from clothes, ornaments, and the body, making the whole area illuminated at once like the moon and the sun, creating a single mass of radiance, a single light.

"Ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi" means he stood at one side, in one place.

"Etadavoca" means he spoke these words such as "Bhikkhu, bhikkhu."

Why did this deity speak using only the term "Bhikkhu" without paying homage? It was because he acted out of the perception of being a monk (samaṇa). It is said that he thought thus: "This person lived in the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) during the interval. But I have been a brahmacārī (holy practitioner) since that time." Thus, the perception of being a monk arose in him; therefore, he spoke using only the term "Bhikkhu" without paying homage.

It is said that this deity was a former companion of the Elder. From what time? From the time of Kassapa Sammasambuddha. Among the five companions who practiced together in the past, the one who was said to be the junior elder (anuthero) and became a Non-returner (Anāgāmī) on the fourth day is this deity. At that time, among them, the Saṅgha Elder attained Arahantship along with the supernormal powers (abhiññā). That Elder, thinking "My task is completed," flew into the sky, washed his face at Lake Anotatta, brought alms-food from Uttarakuru, and said, "Friends, eat this alms-food and practice the Dhamma of a monk without negligence." The others said, "Friend, we do not have such an agreement that 'Whoever first attains distinction and brings alms-food, the others shall eat what he brought and practice the Dhamma of a monk.' You..."
33:
“Venerable Sirs, you have reached the completion of the monk’s task through the support of your own perfections (pāramī). We too, if there is the support of our perfections, shall reach the completion of the monk’s task. Speaking like this is a hindrance and a delay for us; may you, Venerable Sirs, proceed to a place of comfort.” Thus they said. That Great Arahant Elder proceeded to a place of comfort and, at the end of his life span, attained Parinibbāna.

On the following day, the junior elder (Anuthera) realized the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and the higher knowledges (abhiññā) came to him. That Non-returner Elder also brought alms-food in the same manner, but being refused by those monks, he went to a place of comfort and, at the end of his life span, was reborn in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa). That Non-returner Brahma, while staying in the Pure Abodes, looked upon those companions and saw that one had already attained Parinibbāna, one had now reached the Noble ground (ariyabhūmi) in the presence of the Blessed One, and one, depending on gain and honor, had given rise to the thought, ‘I am an Arahant,’ and was living at the port of Suppāraka. Seeing this, he approached him and urged him, saying: “You are not an Arahant, nor are you practicing the path to Arahantship. Go, approach the Blessed One and listen to the Dhamma.” That Bāhiya, having requested an instruction from the Blessed One in the middle of the village, was exhorted by the Blessed One with a brief instruction: “Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: In the seen, let there be only the seen” (Udāna 10). When he was thus exhorted, he reached the Noble ground.

Then, looking to see where the other one was, he saw him living in the Andhavana forest, fulfilling the practice of a trainee (sekhapaṭipadā). He thought: “I will go to the presence of my companion. But when going, it is not proper to go empty-handed; I should take some gift. My companion, while living on the mountain top free from material things, did not even consume the alms-food I offered while standing in the air, but practiced the recluse’s Dhamma. Now, how will he accept a material gift? I will go taking a gift of Dhamma.” Thus thinking, while still staying in the Brahma world, as if stringing a garland of jewels, he analyzed fifteen questions and, taking that Dhamma gift, came and stood not far from his companion. By the power of his habit as a monk, without bowing to that elder, he addressed him, “Bhikkhu, Bhikkhu,” and spoke the words beginning with “This anthill.” In that passage, the repetition “Bhikkhu, Bhikkhu” should be understood as being said with the intent of calling out quickly. Alternatively, just as a forehead is not beautiful with only a single mark (tilaka), but shines as if blossoming and decorated when other marks are given surrounding it, so speech is not beautiful with only a single word, but with a surrounding word...
34:
...it shines as if blossoming and decorated. Intending to make the speech like a blossoming decoration by the power of that surrounding word, he said, “Bhikkhu, Bhikkhu.”

In saying, “This is an anthill,” although there is no actual anthill standing in front, he said “this” as if showing an anthill standing in front by the power of the teaching. “Laṅgī” refers to the door-bolt (or bar) found when digging with a tool. “Wise one, lift up the laṅgī, dig further” means that what is called a laṅgī smokes by night and flames by day; lift that bolt and continue digging further. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all the terms. “Uddhumāyika” refers to a frog. “Caṅkavāra” refers to a water-strainer. “Kumma” refers to a tortoise. “Asisūna” refers to both the meat-cleaver and the chopping block. “Maṃsapesi” refers to a piece of raw meat the size of a small grindstone.

He saw a Naga serpent with a large hood like a cluster of jasmine flowers, encircled by three rings on its neck. “Do not harm the Naga” means he should not harm the Naga by throwing a stick, a vine-end, or dust. “Pay respect to the Naga” means moving away from the windward side, wearing clean clothes, and performing an act of respect to the Naga. The wealth guarded by a Naga does not run out even if consumed for seven generations; the Naga will give you that stored wealth, therefore, pay respect to the Naga—this is the meaning.

“Hearing from here or...” is not like the use of the ablative case (pañcamī vibhatti) in the Dukkhakkhandha Sutta meaning “from this Dispensation,” but here the ablative is used in reference to the deity (devaputta). Therefore, “hearing from me” is the meaning here.

“Consisting of the four great elements” is a name for the body. Just as an external anthill is called “vammika” for four reasons: (1) because it emits (vamati) various creatures such as snakes, mongooses, rats, and house lizards; (2) because it is built (vantaka) by termites; (3) because it is raised (ussita) to the height of a person’s waist or a full human height by termites spitting out dust from their mouths; (4) because it is bound (vantasiṇehasambandha) by the moisture of the termites' saliva so that it does not crumble even when it rains for seven weeks, and even in the dry season, moisture comes out when a handful of dust from it is squeezed. In the same way, this body...
35:
It is called 'Vammika' (an anthill) because it exudes various kinds of impure filth, following the method such as 'eye-wax from the eyes.' It is also called 'Vammika' in the sense of being something discarded by the Noble Ones, because the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants have gone away after discarding this physical body (attabhāva) by exhausting all attachment to it. Furthermore, it is called 'Vammika' as 'Vantussaya' (a heap of discarded things) because this entire body—propped up by three hundred bones, bound by nerves, smeared with flesh, covered with moist skin, and made attractive by the outer skin to deceive beings—is indeed something discarded by the Noble Ones. It is also called 'Vammika' as 'Vantasiṇehasambaddha' (bound by discarded moisture) because it is produced by craving, as it is said: 'Craving brings a man to birth, and his mind runs to and fro' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.55), and because it is bound by the moisture of craving which has been discarded by the Noble Ones.

Just as within an anthill, various kinds of insects are born, pass excrement and urine, lie sick, and die and fall; thus, that anthill serves as their maternity ward, toilet, hospital, and cemetery. In the same way, without considering that this body of Khattiyas and great wealthy men is guarded, protected, adorned, and decorated, and is the body of those with great power, eighty thousand families of worms—classified as those dependent on the outer skin, the skin, the flesh, the nerves, the bones, and the bone marrow—are born within the body itself, pass excrement and urine, lie afflicted with disease, and die and fall. Thus, this body also becomes the maternity ward, toilet, hospital, and cemetery for those worms, and so it has come to be known as 'Vammika.' Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Vammika, monk, is a designation for this body consisting of the four great elements.'

'Mātāpettikasambhava' means being produced from the semen and blood originating from the mother and father. 'Odanakummāsūpacaya' means being nourished and grown by boiled rice and gruel. In the phrase 'Aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhamma,' this body is of an impermanent nature (anicca) because it ceases to exist after having arisen. It is of a nature to be anointed (ucchādana) with perfumes to remove foul odors. It is of a nature to be massaged (parimaddana) by minor kneading to remove the pains of the limbs and body parts. Or, it is of a nature to be massaged by stretching and squeezing to properly shape those limbs that were poorly formed due to being placed on the thighs or staying in the womb during infancy. Even when cared for in this way, it is of a nature to break and be dissolved; it breaks and scatters. This is the inherent nature of the body.
36:
Among those terms, the origin (of the body) is stated by the words: being born of parents, being nourished by rice and gruel, anointing, and massaging. The cessation is stated by the words: impermanence, breaking, and dissolution. Thus, it should be understood that by these seven terms, the high and low states, the growth and decay, and the origin and cessation of the body consisting of the four great elements are described.

'Divā kammante' means the work to be done by day. In the term 'Dhūmāyanā,' the word 'dhūma' (smoke/fume) occurs in these meanings: anger, craving, thought (vitakka), the five cords of sensual pleasure, Dhamma teaching, and literal smoke. In the passage 'Anger is smoke, and lying is ashes' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.165), it refers to anger. In 'Beings are fuming with desire,' it refers to craving. In 'At that time, a certain monk sat fuming (thinking) not far from the Blessed One,' it refers to thought (vitakka).

'Sensual pleasures are a bog and a quagmire,
And this I call a triple-rooted fear;
Dust and smoke have been revealed by me,
Leave them, Brahmadatta, and go forth.' (Jā. 1.6.14) —
In this verse, it refers to the five cords of sensual pleasure. In the passage 'One becomes a smoke-maker,' it refers to Dhamma teaching. In 'A banner is the sign of a chariot, smoke is the sign of fire' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.72), it refers to literal smoke. In this Sutta, however, this word 'dhūma' is intended as thought (vitakka). Therefore, He said: 'This is fuming (thinking) by night.'

'Tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ' means that the Tathāgata is called a 'Brāhmaṇa' because he has expelled seven things. As He said: 'Monk, because of having expelled seven things, one is called a Brāhmaṇa. What seven? Lust is expelled, hatred... delusion... conceit... identity view... doubt... and attachment to rites and rituals are expelled. Monk, because of having expelled these seven things, one is called a Brāhmaṇa.' 'Sumedha' means one of excellent wisdom. In the term 'Sekkhassa,' one is called a 'Sekha' (trainee) because one is training. As He said: 'Monk, he is called a Sekha because he trains. In what does he train? He trains in higher virtue (adhisīla), he trains in higher mind (adhicitta), and he trains in higher wisdom (adhipaññā).'
37:
## The name 'wisdom' (paññā) refers to mundane and supramundane wisdom; it is not the name of a physical weapon. The exertion of energy (vīriya) refers to physical and mental energy. That energy simply follows wisdom. When associated with mundane wisdom, it is mundane energy; when associated with supramundane wisdom, it is supramundane energy. To explain the meaning in this context—

It is heard that a country Brahmin would leave the village early in the morning with his young pupils, spend the day in the forest teaching the Vedas, and return to the village in the evening. On the way, there was a termite mound (vammika). This termite mound would smoke at night and glow by day. The Brahmin said to his resident pupil, the youth Sumedha: "Dear son, this termite mound smokes at night and glows by day; let us see its transformation. Dig it up, divide it into four parts, and throw them away."

Saying "Very well," the youth took a hoe and, standing on the ground with his feet level, did as the Brahmin had said.

In this analogy, the teacher Brahmin is like the Buddha. The youth Sumedha is like a monk in training (sekha). The termite mound is like the physical body. The time when the Brahmin said, "Dear son, this termite mound smokes at night and glows by day; let us see its transformation; dig it up, divide it into four parts, and throw them away," is like the time when the Buddha said, "Monk, divide this body composed of the four great elements into four parts and discern them." The youth's acceptance, saying "Very well," and taking the hoe to do so, is like the sekha monk discerning the body through the definition of the four elements: "The quality of hardness in the twenty parts is the earth element (pathavī-dhātu). The quality of cohesion in the twelve parts is the water element (āpo-dhātu). The quality of maturation (heat) in the four parts is the fire element (tejo-dhātu). The quality of support (motion) in the six parts is the air element (vāyo-dhātu)."

"Monk, 'the bolt' (laṅgī) is a term for ignorance (avijjā)." Why did the Buddha show ignorance as a bolt? Just as when a city gate is closed and the bolt is secured, the movement of the people is cut off—those inside must remain inside, and those outside must remain outside—likewise, for one upon whose gateway of knowledge the bolt of ignorance falls, the movement of knowledge that leads to Nibbāna is cut off. Therefore, He showed ignorance as a bolt. In the phrase "Abandon ignorance," the abandoning of ignorance through the learning and questioning of meditation subjects is described.
38:
Monks, in this word "uddhumāyikā," the frog called uddhumāyika is not very large, being only about the size of a fingernail. It lives among old leaves, in thickets, or among creepers. When that frog is touched with the tip of a stick, the end of a vine, or with dust, it exerts itself and becomes large and round, about the size of a ripe bael fruit (beluva). With its four legs turned toward the sky, its movement is cut off, and it falls under the power of its enemies, becoming mere food for crows, hawks, and the like.

In the same way, when this anger (kodha) first arises, it is merely a disturbance of the mind. If it is not suppressed at that moment, it increases and leads to facial grimacing. If not suppressed then, it leads to the shaking of the jaw. If not suppressed then, it leads to the uttering of harsh speech. If not suppressed then, it leads to looking around in all directions. If not suppressed then, it leads to pulling and dragging. If not suppressed then, it leads to grasping clods of earth, sticks, or weapons with the hand. If not suppressed then, it leads to striking with sticks or weapons. If not suppressed then, it leads to the killing of others or the killing of oneself.

This has also been said: "Since this anger kills others and kills oneself, to this extent, this anger has reached extreme abundance and has attained extreme magnitude."

In that explanation, just as when the four legs of the uddhumāyika frog are turned toward the sky, its movement is cut off and it falls under the power of enemies to become food for crows and so on; even so, a person possessed of anger is unable to take up and develop a meditation subject. He falls under the power of enemies and becomes one who can be treated according to the whims of all the Māras. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Monk, 'uddhumāyikā' is a term for anger and despair (kodhūpāyāsa)." In that context, only anger that has reached great strength is called kodhūpāyāsa. In the phrase "Abandon anger and despair," abandoning through reflection (paṭisaṅkhāna-pahāna) is described.

In the word "dvidhāpatha" (the fork in the road), the analogy is as follows: A man with wealth and possessions, having set out on a desert journey, reaches a fork in the road. Being unable to decide, "Should I go by this way, or should I go by that way?" he stands right there. Then robbers rise up and bring that man to ruin and destruction. Even so, a monk who sits having taken up a basic meditation subject, when doubt (kaṅkhā) arises concerning the Buddha and so forth, is unable to develop the meditation subject. Then all the Māras, such as the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra), bring that monk to ruin and destruction. Thus, indecision (vicikicchā) is like a fork in the road. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Monk, 'dvidhāpatha' is..."
39:
The term 'fork in the road' is a designation for 'doubt' (vicikicchā). In the phrase 'Abandon doubt,' the abandonment of doubt through the power of learning and questioning the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is spoken of.

In the simile of the 'water-strainer' (caṅgavāra), just as when washermen pour water into a strainer, even if it be one pot, two, ten, twenty, or even a hundred pots, the water simply leaks out and not even a handful remains; in the same way, wholesome states (kusaladhamma) do not remain within a person possessed by the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Monk, "water-strainer" is a designation for the five hindrances.' In the phrase 'Abandon the five hindrances,' the abandonment of the hindrances by way of suppression (vikkhambhana) and substitution of opposites (tadaṅga) is spoken of.

In the simile of the 'tortoise' (kumma), just as a tortoise has only five limbs—the four legs and the head; in the same way, when all conditioned things (saṅkhata-dhamma) are grasped together, they are only the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha). Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Monk, "tortoise" is a designation for the five aggregates of clinging.' In the phrase 'Abandon the five aggregates of clinging,' the abandonment of desire and lust (chandarāga) for the five aggregates is spoken of.

In the simile of the 'meat-block' (asisūnā), just as meat is placed on a block and chopped with a knife; in the same way, these beings, for the sake of objective sensuality (vatthukāma), are slaughtered by defilement-sensuality (kilesakāma), and being placed upon objective sensuality, they are sliced and chopped by defilement-sensuality. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Monk, "meat-block" is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure (kāmaguna).' In the phrase 'Abandon the five cords of sensual pleasure,' the abandonment of desire and lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is spoken of.

In the simile of the 'piece of meat' (maṃsapesi), this piece of meat is desired by many people such as kings, and even by animals such as crows. These beings, intoxicated by ignorance (avijjā), approaching delight and lust (nandirāga), prolong the cycle of rebirth (vaṭṭa). Or, just as a piece of meat sticks to wherever it is placed, in the same way, these beings, bound by delight and lust, stick to the cycle of rebirth; even when they encounter suffering, they do not become weary of it. Thus, delight and lust are like a piece of meat. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Monk, "piece of meat" is a designation for delight and lust.' In the phrase 'Abandon delight and lust,' the abandonment of delight and lust by the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga) is spoken of.

In the phrase 'Monk, "Nāga" is a designation for a monk whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava),' the reason why an Arahant is called a 'Nāga' has already been explained in the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta. 'Pay homage to the Nāga' means pay homage to the Buddha-Nāga, whose taints are destroyed.
40:
'That Blessed One is enlightened; he teaches the Dhamma for enlightenment. That Blessed One is tamed; he teaches the Dhamma for taming. That Blessed One is at peace; he teaches the Dhamma for peace. That Blessed One has crossed over; he teaches the Dhamma for crossing over. That Blessed One is extinguished; he teaches the Dhamma for extinction.' Pay homage in this way—this is the meaning here. Thus, this sutta became the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) for the Elder. The Elder, having made this very sutta his meditation subject and developing insight (vipassanā), attained the fruit of Arahantship. 'This is the meaning of this problem' refers to the meaning of this very question. Thus, the Blessed One concluded the teaching according to the sequence, like one taking a gem from a heap of jewels.

## The Commentary on the Vammika Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Rathavinīta Sutta

'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so forth is the Rathavinīta Sutta. Therein, 'at Rājagaha' means in the city of that name. It is called 'Rājagaha' because it was occupied and inhabited by kings such as Mandhātu and Mahāgovinda. Other teachers also explain this in other ways here. What is the use of those explanations? It is merely the name of that city. That city is a city only during the time of a Buddha and the time of a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch). At other times, it is empty, occupied by Yakkhas, and remains as a forest where they dwell. In the phrase 'at the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground' (Veḷuvane Kalandakanivāpe), 'Veḷuvana' is the name of that garden. It is said that the garden was surrounded by bamboo and a wall eighteen cubits high. It is called 'Veḷuvana' because it was endowed with gates and watchtowers, had a dark green appearance, and was delightful. It is called 'Kalandakanivāpa' because a feeding place was given to squirrels there.

In the past, a certain king came there to play in the garden and, being intoxicated with liquor, fell asleep during the day. His attendants, saying 'The king is asleep,' were lured by flowers, fruits, and so forth, and went here and there. Then, attracted by the smell of liquor, a cobra came out from a hollow tree and approached the king. Seeing this, a tree deity thought, 'I will give life to the king,' and having come in the form of a black squirrel, made a sound near his ear. The king woke up.
41:
The cobra turned back. Seeing this, the king thought, "This squirrel has given me my life," and began providing food for the black squirrels in that garden and proclaimed it a sanctuary. Therefore, from that time on, that garden came to be known as "Kalandakanivāpa" (the place where food is given to black squirrels). "Kalandaka" is the name for black squirrels.

"Jātibhūmika" refers to those living in the birthplace. In this context, "Jātibhūmi" means the place of birth. This birthplace is not called "Jātibhūmi" in the sense of the birthplace of King Kosala and others, the Brahmin Caṅkī and others, Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, and other deities, the eighty great disciples, or other beings. Only the Sakyan country, the Kapilavatthu region, which was the birthplace of the Omniscient Bodhisatta—on whose birthday the ten thousand world systems were fragrant with the scent of pollen spread by a single banner of flowers, appearing as beautiful as the Nandana grove in full bloom, and trembling like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, and where many miracles such as the blind gaining sight occurred—is called "Jātibhūmi."

## Description of Revering the Dhamma

"Vassaṃvuṭṭha" refers to those who have completed the three-month rainy season retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony. The Blessed One, after performing the duties of a host with words such as "Monks, is it tolerable?" and so on, spoke the words "Monks, who is...?" and so forth. When those monks were asked by way of greeting (paṭisanthāra), "Monks, is it tolerable? Is it livable? Have you arrived on your journey without much fatigue? Did you not struggle for almsfood? And from where, monks, have you come?", they replied, "Venerable Sir, we have come from the Sakyan country, from the Kapilavatthu region, which is the birthplace (Jātibhūmi)." Then, the Blessed One did not ask about the health of King Suddhodana, Sakkodana, Sukkodana, Dhotodana, Amitodana, Queen Amittā, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, or the entire Sakyan assembly. Instead, wishing to ask about a monk who was endowed with practice, who had himself attained the ten subjects of talk (kathāvatthu) and encouraged others in them, he spoke the words, "Monks, who is...?" and so forth.
42:
## Why did the Blessed One ask about the health of such a monk instead of asking about the health of King Suddhodana and others?

It is because of affection. Indeed, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who are practitioners are dear and pleasing to the Buddhas. For what reason? Because of reverence for the Dhamma. The Tathāgata Buddhas revere the Dhamma. This reverence for the Dhamma should be understood through the aspiration that arose at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree: "It is painful to live without respect and without reliance." Because of reverence for the Dhamma, the Blessed One traveled a distance of three gāvutas to welcome the Elder Mahākassapa on the day of his renunciation. He traveled a distance of over a hundred yojanas to preach the Dhamma on the banks of the Ganges and established King Mahākappina and his retinue in the fruit of Arahantship. One afternoon, he traveled forty-five yojanas to the house of a potter, preached the Dhamma for the three watches of the night, and established the young man Pukkusāti in the fruit of Anāgāmī. He traveled a hundred and twenty yojanas to support the novice Vanavāsī. He traveled sixty yojanas to preach the Dhamma to the Elder Khadiravaniya. 

Knowing that the Elder Anuruddha, staying in the Pācīnavaṃsa forest, was reflecting on the thoughts of a great man, he went there through the air, descended before the Elder, and uttered words of praise (Sādhu). He arranged a lodging for the Elder Koṭikaṇṇa Soṇa in the same Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), requested him to preach the Dhamma at dawn, and uttered words of praise at the conclusion of the intonation (sarabhañña). He traveled three gāvutas to the Gosingasālavana forest where three young men lived and spoke on the benefits of unity. The Blessed One Kassapa also, having developed confidence that "This is a noble disciple established in the fruit of Anāgāmī," went to the house of the potter Ghaṭīkāra and, taking food with his own hands, partook of it.

Our Blessed One also, when the time for the rainy season retreat was near, set out on a journey from Jetavana Monastery accompanied by the Saṅgha of monks. King Kosala, Anāthapiṇḍika, and others were unable to stop him from leaving. When Anāthapiṇḍika returned home, he sat down in distress. Then a servant girl named Puṇṇā asked, "Master, why are you distressed?" He replied, "Yes, girl, I was unable to stop the Teacher from leaving. Therefore, I will not have the opportunity to hear the Dhamma or give alms as I wish during these three months of the rainy season." She said, "Master, I too will try to stop the Teacher from leaving." He said, "If you can stop him, I will free you from slavery." Puṇṇā went, prostrated at the feet of the Ten-Powered One, and said, "Blessed One, please return." The Blessed One said, "Puṇṇā, you are one whose life is dependent on others; what can you do for me?"
43:
"Venerable Sir, you also know that I have no gift to offer. However, because of your turning back, I shall establish myself in the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts," she said. The Blessed One, saying "Sādhu, sādhu, Puṇṇā," gave his approval, turned back, and entered Jetavana Monastery. This story became well-known. When the great merchant heard that "the Blessed One turned back because of Puṇṇā," he freed her from slavery and placed her in the position of a daughter. She requested ordination, became a nun, and practiced Vipassanā. Then, the Teacher, knowing that she had undertaken Vipassanā, uttered this verse of radiance:

"Puṇṇā, you have fulfilled the Good Dhamma, like the moon on the fifteenth day.
With perfected wisdom, you shall make an end of suffering."

At the end of the verse, she attained the Fruit of Arahantship and became a well-known female disciple. In this way, the Tathāgatas hold the Dhamma in high regard.

Even while the Venerable Nandaka was preaching the Dhamma in the assembly hall, the Blessed One, without having bathed, went there and stood for all three watches of the night listening to the Dhamma talk, and at the end of the teaching, he gave his approval (Sādhu). The Elder came, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable Sir, at what time did you arrive?" "I arrived just as you began the Sutta," he replied. "Venerable Sir, you have performed a difficult task; you Buddhas are delicate and refined," he said. "Nandaka, if you were able to preach for an aeon, I would listen even while standing for an aeon," the Blessed One said. In this way, the Tathāgatas hold the Dhamma in high regard. Because they hold the Dhamma in high regard, those who practice it are beloved to them; therefore, he asked about the practitioners. There are four types of practitioners (paṭipannaka): one who practices for one's own benefit but not for the benefit of others; one who practices for the benefit of others but not for one's own benefit; one who practices neither for one's own benefit nor for the benefit of others; and one who practices both for one's own benefit and for the benefit of others.

Among these four, one who, like the Venerable Bākula, personally possesses the ten subjects of discourse but does not advise or instruct others with those teachings, is called one who practices for one's own benefit but not for the benefit of others. The Blessed One does not ask about such a monk. Why? Because he does not stand on the side of the growth of my Dispensation (Sāsana).

One who does not personally possess the ten subjects of discourse but advises others with those teachings, like Upananda the Sakyan, for the sake of receiving the services performed by others, this person [practices] for the benefit of others...
44:
As for one who does not practice for his own benefit but practices only for the benefit of others, the Buddha does not ask about such a person. Why? Because for that monk, craving has not yet been abandoned, like a large basket. 

One who does not himself possess the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu) and does not instruct others with those teachings (like Lāḷudāyī) is called one who practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others. The Buddha does not ask about such a person either. Why? Because within that person, the defilements are as numerous as large tree stumps cut with an axe. 

One who himself possesses the ten subjects of discourse and also instructs others with those teachings is called one who practices for both his own benefit and the benefit of others (like the eighty great elders such as Venerable Sāriputta, Venerable Moggallāna, and Venerable Mahākassapa). The Blessed One asks about such a monk. Why? Because he is considered as "one who stands on the side of the growth and progress of my Dispensation". In this sutta as well, wishing to ask only about such a monk, he said: "Monks, who is...?" and so forth. 

When the Blessed One asked those monks about a monk in their own native land who practices for both his own benefit and the benefit of others and who possesses the ten subjects of discourse, saying "Who is such a person there?", there was no need for them to think or consult among themselves. Why? Because Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta was as famous and well-known in that district as the moon or the sun positioned in the middle of the sky. Therefore, like flocks of peacocks gathering together upon hearing the sound of thunder, or like energetic monks, when reporting about their teacher Venerable Puṇṇa to the Blessed One, they were unable to finish speaking of the Elder's virtues and thus said all at once: "Venerable Sir, the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta..." and so forth. In that statement, "Puṇṇa" is the name of that Elder. Because he was the son of the Brahmin lady Mantāṇī, he is called "Mantāṇiputta". "Sambhāvita" means one who is esteemed because his virtues are praised.

## Explanation of Fewness of Wishes and so forth

"Appiccha" (one with few wishes) means one who is free from desire, without longing, and devoid of craving. Here, although the phrasing (byañjana) might seem incomplete, the meaning (attha) is complete without remainder. This is because there is not even the slightest evil desire within that Venerable One. He is an Arahant who has entirely abandoned craving. Furthermore, in this context, the distinctions between excessive desire (atricchatā), evil desire (pāpicchatā), great desire (mahicchatā), and fewness of wishes (appicchatā) should be understood.
45:
Among those varieties, the longing for the gains of others while being dissatisfied with one's own gains is called atricchatā (excessive desire). To one possessed of such excessive desire, even a cake cooked in a single pan appears as if it were poorly cooked or small when it falls into his own bowl. Yet, when that same cake is placed in another's bowl, it appears as if it were well-cooked or large. Pretending to possess virtues that one does not have and lacking moderation in receiving requisites is called pāpicchatā (evil desire). This evil desire is indeed mentioned in the Abhidhamma in this manner: "Here, a certain person, being without faith, desires, 'Let people know me as one who has faith,'" and so on. A person possessed of such evil desire stands in hypocrisy (kohaṇña). Wanting others to know the virtues that one actually possesses and lacking moderation in receiving requisites is called mahicchatā (great desire). This great desire is also mentioned in the Vibhaṅga as follows: "Here, a certain person, being faithful, desires, 'Let people know me as one who has faith'; being virtuous, he desires, 'Let people know me as one who is virtuous,'" and so on. A person possessed of such great desire is difficult to satisfy. Even his own biological mother cannot satisfy his mind. Therefore, it is said:

"A great mass of fire, the ocean, and a person of great desire—even if one were to provide them with requisites by the cartload, these three are insatiable."

Desiring to conceal the virtues one possesses and knowing moderation in receiving requisites is called appicchatā (fewness of wishes). A person possessed of such fewness of wishes, because of the desire to hide the virtues present in himself, does not desire, "Though I have faith, let people know me as one who has faith." Though he is virtuous, secluded, learned, energetic, possessed of concentration, wise, and an Arahant whose taints are exhausted, he does not desire, "Let people know me as an Arahant." He is like the Elder Majjhantika.

That Elder was indeed a great Arahant, yet his bowl and robes were worth only a small fraction (a pè). He was the Presiding Elder (Saṅghatthera) on the day of the great monastery dedication (vihāramaha) of King Asoka the Righteous. Then, seeing his very shabby appearance, people said, "Venerable Sir, please step outside for a moment." The Elder thought, "If an Arahant like me does not support the King, who else will?" and dived into the earth, only to emerge while receiving the alms-food offered to the Presiding Elder. Thus, though he was an Arahant, he did not desire, "Let people know me as an Arahant." Such a monk of few wishes can bring about gains not yet received and make firm the gains already received.
46:
(That monk) gladdens the hearts of the donors. Indeed, because of his fewness of wishes, in whatever way he accepts a small amount of requisites, in that same way, people who are inspired by his practice give many things.

Furthermore, fewness of wishes (appiccha) is of four kinds: fewness of wishes regarding requisites (paccaya-appicchatā), fewness of wishes regarding ascetic practices (dhutaṅga-appicchatā), fewness of wishes regarding learning (pariyatti-appicchatā), and fewness of wishes regarding attainments (adhigama-appicchatā). Among these four, one who has few wishes regarding the four requisites is called paccaya-appicchatā. Such a monk who has few wishes regarding requisites knows the donor's wish, knows the measure of the gift, and knows his own capacity. If the gift is abundant but the donor wishes to give only a little, he accepts only a little according to the donor's wish. If the gift is small but the donor wishes to give much, he accepts only a little according to the measure of the gift. If the gift is abundant and the donor also wishes to give much, he knows his own capacity and accepts only in moderation.

One who does not want others to know that he has undertaken ascetic practices is called dhutaṅga-appicchatā. To illustrate this meaning, there are these stories: The Elder Mahāsumana, who practiced the cemetery-dweller's practice, lived in a cemetery for sixty years, and not even another single monk knew of it. Therefore, it is said:

"I lived continuously in the cemetery for sixty years.
Let not a second person know of me; oh, what a noble cemetery-dweller!"

Two brothers who were Elders lived on the Cetiyapabbata mountain. Among them, the younger Elder took pieces of sugarcane sent by a supporter and went to the elder brother. He said, "Venerable Sir, please consume this." It was the time when the Elder had finished his meal and was washing his face. That Elder said, "Enough, friend." The younger asked, "Venerable Sir, are you perhaps a one-session eater (ekāsanika)?" (Then the elder brother), desiring to hide his ascetic practice although he had been a one-session eater for fifty years, said, "Friend, bring the sugarcane," and after consuming it and washing his face, he re-undertook the practice and departed.

One who, like the Elder Sāketaka Tissa, does not want others to know of his great learning is called pariyatti-appicchatā. That Elder, saying "There is no time," did not give opportunity for instruction and inquiry. When urged, "Venerable Sir, you will attain the end of death (Nibbāna)," he left his group of disciples and went to the Kaṇikāravālikasamudda Vihāra. In that monastery, throughout the rainy season, he was of service to the senior, middle, and junior monks...
47:
(That Elder) having become so, on the full moon Uposatha day of the Mahāpavāraṇā, he departed after stirring the crowd with a Dhamma discourse.

One who, being one of the noble ones such as a Sotāpanna, does not wish to let others know of his status as a Sotāpanna and so forth, is called "Adhigama-appiccha" (one with fewness of wishes regarding attainments). This is like the three clansmen [Anuruddha, etc.] or Ghaṭīkāra the potter.

The Venerable Puṇṇa, however, having abandoned excessive desire, evil desire, and great desire, was called "Appiccha" (one with few wishes) because he was endowed with pure fewness of wishes, known as non-greed, which is the opposite of desire. He also said to the monks: "Friends, these states—excessive desire, evil desire, and great desire—must be abandoned." Showing the danger in those desires, he gave a talk on fewness of wishes (appiccha-kathā), saying: "One should undertake and practice such fewness of wishes." Therefore, it was said: "He is himself one of few wishes and is one who speaks to the monks on fewness of wishes."

## Explanation of the Twelvefold Contentment (Santosa)

Now, in the phrases "He is himself content" and so forth, I shall explain only the specific meanings. The connection of sentences (yojanā) should be understood in the manner already stated. "Santosa" (contentment) means being endowed with contentment with whatever requisites one receives. That contentment is of twelve kinds. They are: three kinds regarding robes—contentment with what one gets (yathālābha-santosa), contentment according to one's strength (yathābala-santosa), and contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppa-santosa). The same applies to alms-food and other requisites. The detailed explanation of these types of contentment is as follows:

In this Dispensation, a monk receives a robe, whether it is good or bad. He is satisfied with that alone and does not desire another; even if he could receive more, he does not take it. This is his contentment with what he gets (yathālābha-santosa) regarding robes. Furthermore, if a monk is naturally weak or is oppressed by illness and old age, he becomes exhausted when wearing a heavy robe. If he exchanges that robe with a suitable fellow monk and is satisfied with a light one, he is still considered content. This is his contentment according to strength (yathābala-santosa) regarding robes. Another monk is one who receives excellent requisites. When he receives a certain expensive robe such as a silk robe, or many robes, he gives them away, thinking: "This is suitable for senior elders of long standing; this is appropriate for those of great learning; let this be for those who are sick; let this be for those who receive few gains." Then, taking their old robes...
48: ...or picking up rags from dust heaps and the like, making a double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) with those rags and wearing it, he is still one who is content. This is his "contentment with what is suitable" (yathāsāruppa-santosa) regarding robes. In this Dispensation, a monk receives alms-food, whether it is coarse or fine. That monk is satisfied with only that obtained food; he does not long for other food, and even if he receives it, he does not accept it. This is his "contentment with what is obtained" (yathālābha-santosa) regarding alms-food. A monk who receives alms-food that is unsuitable for his natural constitution or unsuitable for his illness, such that he would be uncomfortable if he consumed it, gives that food to a compatible monk and, eating suitable food from that monk's hand, continues to practice the recluse's Dhamma; he is still one who is content. This is his "contentment according to one's strength" (yathābala-santosa) regarding alms-food. Another monk receives much fine alms-food. Just as with the robes, he gives it to senior monks, learned monks, monks with few gains, and sick monks, and he is content even if he eats their leftovers or eats mixed food obtained by wandering for alms. This is his "contentment with what is suitable" (yathāsāruppa-santosa) regarding alms-food. In this Dispensation, a monk receives a lodging (senāsana), whether it is pleasant or unpleasant. That monk does not give rise to joy because of that lodging, nor does he give rise to resentment; he is content with whatever is obtained, even if it is at least a grass mat. This is his "contentment with what is obtained" (yathālābha-santosa) regarding lodging. A monk who receives a lodging that is unsuitable for his natural constitution or unsuitable for his illness, such that he would be uncomfortable while staying there, gives that lodging to a compatible monk and, staying in a suitable lodging belonging to that monk, he is still one who is content. This is his "contentment according to one's strength" (yathābala-santosa) regarding lodging. Another monk of great merit receives many fine lodgings such as caves, pavilions, and gabled houses. Just as with the robes and so on, he gives them to senior monks, learned monks, monks with few gains, and sick monks, and he is content staying anywhere. This is his "contentment with what is suitable" (yathāsāruppa-santosa) regarding lodging. Also, a monk who reflects, "Excellent lodging is a ground for negligence; sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) descend upon one sitting there, and when one who is overcome by sleep wakes up again, evil thoughts appear," does not accept such a lodging even when it is reached. Having rejected it, he is content even if he stays in the open air or at the foot of a tree. This also is his "contentment with what is suitable" (yathāsāruppa-santosa) regarding lodging. In this Dispensation, a monk receives medicine, whether it is coarse or fine. That monk is content with only what he receives; he does not long for another, and even if he receives it, he does not accept it. This is his "contentment with what is obtained" (yathālābha-santosa) regarding the requisite of medicine for the sick. A monk who has a need for oil...
49:
If he receives molasses, he gives it to a fellow monk and takes oil from that monk's hand, or seeks other oil, and even while treating his illness with those medicines, he remains content. This is his 'contentment according to strength' (yathābalasantosa) regarding medicinal requisites. Another monk of great merit receives many excellent medicines such as oil, honey, and molasses. Like a robe, he gives them to senior monks, learned monks, monks of few gains, or sick monks, and remains content even while subsisting on whatever medicine they bring back. However, if a monk has gall-nut soaked in urine in one vessel and the four sweet foods (catumadhura) in another, and when told, 'Venerable sir, take what you wish,' he reflects: 'Even though the illness could be cured by either, gall-nut soaked in urine is a medicine praised by the Buddhas and others.' Rejecting the four sweet foods and treating himself only with the gall-nut in urine, he is supremely content. This is his 'contentment according to suitability' (yathāsāruppasantosa) regarding medicinal requisites.

Among these three types of contentment for each of the four requisites, 'contentment according to suitability' is the highest. The Venerable Puṇṇa was content with these three types of contentment in each requisite. Regarding 'talk on contentment' (santuṭṭhikathā), he was one who frequently spoke this talk on contentment to the monks.

## Explanation of the Three Kinds of Seclusion
'One who is secluded' means one endowed with these three kinds of seclusion: physical seclusion (kāyapaviveka), mental seclusion (cittapaviveka), and seclusion from acquisitions (upadhipaviveka). Among them, walking alone, standing alone, sitting alone, lying down alone, entering the village for alms alone, returning alone, undertaking the canopy walk alone, practicing alone, and dwelling alone is called physical seclusion. The eight attainments (samāpatti) are called mental seclusion. Nibbāna is called seclusion from acquisitions. It is also said: 'Physical seclusion is for those whose bodies are secluded and who delight in renunciation. Mental seclusion is for those of purified minds who have reached supreme purity. Seclusion from acquisitions is for those individuals free from acquisitions who have reached the unconditioned (visaṅkhāra),' as stated in the Mahāniddesa. Regarding 'talk on seclusion' (pavivekakathā), he was one who frequently spoke this talk on seclusion to the monks.
50:
## Explanation of the Five Kinds of Entanglement
'Unentangled' (asaṃsaṭṭha) means one who is free from the five kinds of entanglement (saṃsagga). The five kinds of entanglement are: entanglement by hearing (savana-saṃsagga), entanglement by seeing (dassana-saṃsagga), entanglement by conversing (samullapana-saṃsagga), entanglement by enjoying together (sambhoga-saṃsagga), and entanglement by physical contact (kāya-saṃsagga).

Among these, a monk in this Dispensation hears: 'In such-and-such a village or town, there is a woman or a young girl who is very beautiful, lovely, pleasing, and endowed with the highest beauty of complexion.' Having heard this, his heart sinks, he becomes despondent, and is unable to maintain the holy life. Without revealing the weakness of his training, he returns to the lower life. Lust that arises through the process of auditory consciousness, whether by hearing others describe such perfection of form or by hearing the sounds of laughter, talk, or song himself, is called entanglement by hearing. This entanglement by hearing should be understood through the stories of the Bodhisatta who became a Paccekabuddha (Anitthigandha) and the young monk Tissa who lived in Pañcaggaḷa Cave.

It is heard that: While that young monk was traveling through the air, he heard the voice of a goldsmith's daughter from Girigāma village singing in a sweet voice after bathing and wearing lotus flowers at a lotus pond with five other girls. Pierced by sensual lust, his special attainments declined, and he met with ruin.

In this Dispensation, a monk does not merely hear, but himself sees a woman or a young girl who is beautiful, lovely, pleasing, and endowed with the highest beauty of complexion. Having seen her, his heart sinks, he becomes despondent, and is unable to maintain the holy life. Without revealing the weakness of his training, he returns to the lower life. Lust that arises through the process of visual consciousness for a monk looking at an object of the opposite sex is called entanglement by seeing.

This entanglement by seeing should be understood thus: It is heard that a young monk went to Kāladīghavāpidvāra-vihāra for the purpose of study. The teacher, a Thera, seeing the danger to him, did not give him permission. The monk pleaded repeatedly. The teacher said, 'If you will not wander into the village, I will give you the lesson.' He accepted, saying 'Very well.' After finishing the lesson, he paid respects to the teacher and while leaving, thought, 'Why does my teacher forbid me from entering this village?' Wanting to know the reason, he put on his robe and entered the village. A young woman, dressed in yellow cloth, was standing at her house. Seeing the young monk, lust arose in her. She brought gruel with a ladle, poured it into his bowl, returned inside, and lay down on a bed. Then she...
51:
The parents asked, "Dear daughter, what has happened?" She replied, "If I obtain the young monk who just left through the door, I shall live; if not, I shall die." The parents went quickly and, catching up with the young monk at the village gate, they paid homage and said, "Please return, Bhante, and accept almsfood." The young monk replied, "It is enough, let me go." They pleaded, "Bhante, there is a reason for this," and further entreated, "Bhante, there is this much wealth in our house, and we have only one daughter. You shall stay in the position of our eldest son; you can live happily." The young monk, saying, "I have no need for this impediment of household life," paid no heed to their words and departed.

The parents returned home and said, "Dear daughter, we were unable to make the monk return. You shall have any other husband you desire. Please get up, eat, and drink." That young woman, having no such desire, remained without food for seven days and passed away. After performing her funeral rites, the parents offered that golden-colored cloth to the Saṅgha of monks at Dhura-vihāra. The monks cut the cloth into pieces and distributed them. One elder took his portion and came to Kalyāṇī-vihāra. That young monk also went to that same monastery, intending to worship the Cetiya, and sat in a place for daytime rest. The elder monk took that piece of cloth and said to the young monk, "Please prepare a water-strainer for me with this cloth." When the young monk asked, "Venerable Mahāthera, where did you get this cloth?", the elder monk told him the whole story. As soon as the young monk heard those words, he was consumed by the fire of passion, thinking, "I have lost the chance to live with such a woman," and he passed away right there.

Passion that arises through mutual conversation is called samullapana-saṃsagga (association by conversation). Passion that arises because a monk uses the property of a bhikkhunī, or a bhikkhunī uses the property of a monk, is called sambhoga-saṃsagga (association by use of belongings). This sambhoga-saṃsagga should be understood thus: It is said that at the festival of Maricavaṭṭi-vihāra, there were one hundred thousand monks and ninety thousand bhikkhunīs. A certain novice (sāmaṇera), while carrying hot rice gruel, sometimes placed it on the corner of his robe and sometimes set it on the ground. A novice nun (sāmaṇerī), seeing this, gave him a tray, saying, "Place your bowl on this and go." Later, when a danger arose, they went to the other side of the sea. Among them, the bhikkhunī arrived first. Hearing that a Sinhalese monk had arrived, she went to the elder, greeted him, and sat down, asking, "Bhante, how many years (vassa) had you been ordained at the time of the Maricavaṭṭi-vihāra festival?" He replied, "At that time, I was a seven-year-old novice. And how many years had you been?" She replied, "I was also just a seven-year-old novice nun."
52:
"I once gave a tray to a novice who was carrying hot rice gruel to place his bowl on," said the former novice nun. The elder said, "I am that person," and taking the tray out of his bag, he showed it to her. Due to even this much association (saṃsagga), both of them were unable to maintain the holy life (brahmacariya) and disrobed at the age of sixty.

Passion that arises through holding hands and so forth is called kāya-saṃsagga (physical association). In this regard, there is this story: It is said that on the terrace of the Mahācetiya, young monks were reciting their texts. Behind those monks, young bhikkhunīs were listening to the Dhamma. Then, a young monk stretched out his hand and touched the body of a young bhikkhunī. That bhikkhunī took that hand and placed it on her breast. Due to even this much contact, both of them disrobed and returned to lay life.

## Explanation of Gāhagāhaka and Others

Among these five types of association (saṃsagga), for monks among themselves, hearing, seeing, conversing, using things together, and physical contact always occur. With bhikkhunīs, except for physical association (kāya-saṃsagga), the other associations occur from time to time. Similarly, with laymen (upāsaka) and laywomen (upāsikā), all types of association occur from time to time. In such associations, one must guard the mind so that defilements do not arise. One monk is a gāhagāhaka, one is a gāhamuttaka, one is a muttagāhaka, and one is a muttamuttaka.

Among those four types: When people approach a monk by enticing him with material gifts (āmisa), and the monk also approaches them by enticing them with flowers, fruits, and so forth, this monk is called a gāhagāhaka (a taker who is taken). When people approach in the aforementioned way, but the monk approaches them only in the capacity of one worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya), this monk is called a gāhamuttaka (one who is taken but remains free). When people, regarding him as one worthy of offerings, donate the four requisites, but the monk approaches them by enticing them with flowers, fruits, and so forth, this monk is called a muttagāhaka (one who is free but becomes a taker). When people donate the four requisites regarding him as one worthy of offerings, and the monk also makes use of them only in the capacity of one worthy of offerings, like the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātiya Tissa, this monk is called a muttamuttaka (one who is free and remains free).

A certain laywoman (upāsikā) attended to an elder for twelve years. One day, a fire broke out in that village and the houses were burnt to ashes. Other monks who frequented families (kulūpaka)...
53: Other monks arrived and inquired meticulously, "O laywoman, have you been able to keep your small possessions from being destroyed?" The people replied, "The Elder who is our mother's regular object of support will only come at the time of the meal." The Elder, too, having noted the time for alms-round on the following day, arrived. The laywoman had him sit in the shade of the granary, prepared the alms-food, and offered it. When the Elder had finished his meal and departed, the people said again, "The Elder who is our mother's regular object of support comes only at the time of the meal." The laywoman replied, "The monks you regularly support are suitable only for you; my noble Elder is suitable only for me." The Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, through these five types of association, did not mingle with the fourfold assembly; he was both gāhamuttaka (others clung to him, but he did not cling) and muttamuttaka (neither others nor he clung). Just as he himself did not mingle, he was also in the habit of speaking to the monks about such non-mingling. ## Āraddhavīriya (aroused energy) means having exerted effort, being endowed with complete bodily and mental energy. This is the meaning: a monk who does not allow a defilement that has arisen while walking to persist until he stands; who does not allow a defilement that has arisen while standing to persist until he sits; and who does not allow a defilement that has arisen while sitting to persist until he lies down. He lives like one who squeezes and holds a cobra with a mantra, or like one who treads on the neck of an enemy. Such a monk is called one with aroused energy (āraddhavīriya). The Elder was such a person. He was also in the habit of speaking to the monks about the arousal of energy in the same way. In the passages beginning with sīlasampanna (endowed with virtue), sīla refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). Samādhi refers to the eight attainments which are the basis for insight (vipassanā). Paññā refers to mundane and supramundane wisdom. Vimutti refers to the noble fruition (ariyaphala). Vimuttiñāṇadassana refers to the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa). The Elder himself was endowed with virtue and so forth, and he was in the habit of speaking to the monks about virtue and so forth. Because that Elder admonished with the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu), he is called an admonisher (ovādaka). Just as some can only admonish but cannot turn and explain the subtle meaning to make it understood, the Elder was not like that. Because the Elder could make those ten subjects of discourse understood, he is called one who makes others understand (viññāpaka). Some can make things understood but cannot demonstrate the reason; because the Elder could also demonstrate the reason, he is called one who clarifies (sandassaka). Some can demonstrate the evident reason but cannot make others accept it; because the Elder could also make others accept it, he is called one who encourages (samādapaka). In this way,
54:
Because he incites effort by establishing the monks in those subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu), he is called 'Samuttejaka' (one who stimulates). Because he gladdens them by speaking of their virtues when effort has arisen, he is called 'Sampahaṃsaka' (one who inspires).

## Explanation of the Five Gains
'Suladdhalābhā' (well-gained are the gains) means that for others, obtaining qualities such as human existence and ordination are indeed gains. However, for the Venerable Punna, these are well-gained because such fame and praise have spread in the presence of the Teacher. Furthermore, praise from the unwise is not such a gain, but praise from the wise is a true gain. Praise from laypeople is also not such a gain. For when laypeople say, 'I will speak praise,' and say, 'Our noble lord is gentle, amiable, and easy to talk to; he provides hospitality with gruel, rice, molasses, etc., to those who come to the monastery,' they are actually speaking of what is not praiseworthy (avanna). When they wish to disparage, saying, 'This elder is very slow, seems weak, and often frowns; it is not easy to be intimate with him,' they are actually speaking of his virtues (vanna). Praise from fellow practitioners in the absence of the Teacher is also not such a gain, but praise in the presence of the Teacher is a great gain. It is in reference to this meaning that 'Suladdhalābhā' is said. 'Anumassa anumassa' means repeatedly entering into the ten subjects of discourse (to teach). The Teacher also rejoices in that teaching, saying, 'This monk has few wishes, this monk is content,' thus expressing appreciation for the Elder's virtues. Thus, there are five gains: one from the praise of the wise, one from fellow practitioners, one in the presence of the Teacher, one from repeatedly teaching the subjects of discourse, and one from the Teacher's appreciation. It is in reference to these five gains that 'Suladdhalābhā' is said. 'Kadāci' means at some time. 'Karahaci' is a synonym for the same. 'Appeva nāma siyā koccideva kathāsallāpo' means 'perhaps there might be some conversation.' It is said that the Elder Sāriputta had never seen the Venerable Punna before, nor had he heard his Dhamma talk. Thus, desiring to see him and hear his Dhamma talk, he spoke in this way.

## Explanation of Wandering, etc.
'Yathābhirantaṃ' means having stayed as long as one wishes (according to one's inclination). For when Buddhas stay in one place for a long time, there may be a deficiency in shade, water, etc., or the lodgings may become uncomfortable, or for the people...
55:
The Buddhas do not experience what is called a lack of delight (discontent) arising from a lack of faith or similar causes. Nor do they stay for a long time out of excessive delight, thinking, 'Let us dwell happily here,' because of the abundance of such comforts as shade and shelter. Rather, the Buddhas dwell in a place with the intention of establishing beings in those virtues—wherever beings, while the Buddha is residing there, establish themselves in the refuges, undertake the precepts, go forth into monkhood, or where there is a strong supporting condition (upaniśśaya) for them to attain the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) and so forth. When those virtues are absent, they depart. Therefore, it is said, 'Having stayed as long as he wished.'

'While wandering on a journey' refers to traveling a long distance. The Buddha's wandering (cārika) is of two kinds: rapid wandering (turitacārika) and non-rapid (leisurely) wandering (aturitacārika). Among these two, rapid wandering (turitacārika) refers to traveling quickly to enable a person who is ready for enlightenment to realize the Four Noble Truths, even if they are in a distant place. This rapid wandering can be seen in instances such as going to meet the Venerable Mahākassapa. Indeed, the Buddha traveled a distance of three gāvutas in a moment to meet the Venerable Mahākassapa. He traveled thirty yojanas for the ogre Āḷavaka, and similarly (thirty yojanas) for Angulimāla. For Pukkusāti, he traveled forty-five yojanas; for Mahākappina, one hundred and twenty yojanas; for Khadiravaniya (Revata), seven hundred yojanas; and for the novice Vanavāsī Tissa, the co-resident of the Captain of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, he traveled one hundred and twenty yojanas and three gāvutas.

It is said that one day the Elder (Venerable Sāriputta) said, 'Venerable Sir, I shall go to the novice Tissa.' The Buddha said, 'I too will go,' and calling the Venerable Ānanda, he said, 'Ānanda, inform twenty thousand monks who possess the six higher knowledges (saḷabhiññā) that the Buddha will go to the novice Vanavāsī Tissa.' Then, on the second day, surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants (khīṇāsava), he flew through the air and descended at the gate of the alms-village of that novice, one hundred and twenty yojanas away, and donned his robes. When the people going to work saw him, they said, 'Friends, the Teacher has arrived; do not go to work yet.' They prepared seats, offered rice gruel (yāgu), and while performing their duties, they asked the young monks, 'Venerable Sir, where is the Buddha going?' The monks replied, 'Lay followers, the Buddha is not going elsewhere; he has come here to see the novice Tissa.' They were filled with joy, thinking, 'The Teacher has come to see the Elder who is our refuge; our Elder is indeed no ordinary person.'
56:
Then, when the Buddha's meal was finished, the novice wandered into the village for alms and asked, 'Lay followers, is the assembly of monks large?' Then those people informed him, 'Venerable Sir, the Teacher has arrived.' The novice approached the Buddha and invited him with alms-food. The Buddha took the novice's bowl in his hand and said, 'Enough, Tissa, the meal is finished.' After that, the novice invited his preceptor (upajjhāya) with alms-food, and sitting in his designated place, he finished his meal.

Then, when the novice's meal was finished, the Buddha spoke the Maṅgala Sutta, departed from the village, and standing at the village gate, asked, 'Tissa, which is the path to your dwelling place?' When the novice pointed out the path, saying, 'Venerable Sir, it is this path,' the Buddha said, 'Tissa, you go ahead.' Although the Buddha is the guide for the world including the devas, he thought, 'I shall have the opportunity to observe the novice along the entire three-gāvuta path,' and thus made the novice the guide.

The novice went to his dwelling place and performed his duties for the Buddha. Then the Buddha asked him, 'Tissa, where is your walking path (caṅkama)?' and going there, he sat on the novice's stone seat and asked, 'Tissa, do you live happily in this place?' The novice replied, 'Yes, Venerable Sir, as I live in this place and hear the sounds of lions, tigers, elephants, deer, peacocks, and so forth, the perception of the forest (araññasaññā) arises in me; with that perception, I live happily.' Then the Buddha said to him, 'Tissa, assemble the assembly of monks; I shall give you the inheritance of the Buddha.' Having said this, he granted him higher ordination (Upasampadā) in the midst of the assembled Sangha and then returned to his own residence. This is called rapid wandering (turitacārika).

Leisurely wandering (aturitacārika) refers to traveling through villages and market towns in order, at a rate of half a yojana or one yojana per day, benefiting the world through alms-round and other means. While wandering in this manner, the Buddha travels in one of these three circuits: the Great Circuit (Mahāmaṇḍala), the Middle Circuit (Majjhimamaṇḍala), or the Final Circuit (Antimamaṇḍala). Among these circuits, the Great Circuit is nine hundred yojanas, the Middle Circuit is six hundred yojanas, and the Final Circuit is three hundred yojanas in extent. When he wishes to wander in the Great Circuit, he performs the Pavāraṇā on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā and departs on the first day of the waning moon, surrounded by a great assembly of monks. A great commotion arises for a hundred yojanas around; those who arrive first get the opportunity to invite him. The offerings and honors that would occur in the other two circuits converge into the Great Circuit. There, the Buddha stays for one or two days in various villages and market towns, benefiting the great multitude by accepting material offerings and by giving the gift of Dhamma...
57:
While cultivating wholesome states connected to Nibbāna, the escape from the round of suffering, He concludes His wandering in nine months.

If, during the rains-retreat (vassa), the practice of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā) of the monks is still immature, He does not perform the Pavāraṇā on the full moon day of Assayuja, the Great Pavāraṇā day. Instead, after performing the Pavāraṇā-saṅgaha (postponement/brief ceremony), He performs the Pavāraṇā on the full moon day of Kattika. Then, on the first day of the month of Migasīla, He sets out surrounded by a large community of monks and arrives at the Middle Region (Majjhima-maṇḍala). If He wishes to wander in the Middle Region for other reasons, He sets out only after staying for four months. In the same manner as previously mentioned, the offerings that would have been received in the other two regions accumulate only in the Middle Region. The Blessed One, favoring the assembly of beings to be guided (veneyya) in the same manner as before, concludes His wandering in eight months.

If, even after the four months of the rains-retreat have ended, the faculties (indriya) of the beings to be guided are not yet mature, He continues to stay in that very place of retreat for another month, or two, three, or four months, awaiting the maturation of their faculties. Then, He sets out surrounded by a large community of monks. In the same manner as previously mentioned, the offerings that would have been received in the other two regions accumulate only in the Inner Region (Anto-maṇḍala). The Blessed One, favoring the assembly of beings to be guided in the same manner as before, concludes His wandering in seven, six, five, or four months. Thus, when He wanders in any of these three regions, He does not wander for the sake of the four requisites such as robes.

Rather, He wanders out of compassion for the world, thinking: "When will the poor, the foolish, the aged, and the sick be able to come and see the Tathāgata? Only when I wander will the masses have the opportunity to see the Tathāgata. When they see Him, some will gain clarity of mind, some will make offerings of flowers and such, some will offer a spoonful of alms-food, and some will abandon wrong view and become those with right view. Such actions will lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time."

Furthermore, the Blessed Buddhas wander for four reasons: for the physical comfort of the body by means of walking (janghā-vihāra); for the sake of awaiting the appropriate time for an event to arise; for the sake of prescribing training rules (sikkhāpada) for the monks; and for the sake of awakening those beings capable of being awakened (bodheneyya) whose faculties have matured in various places. The Blessed Buddhas also wander for another four reasons: thinking, "They will go to the Buddha for refuge," or "They will go to the Dhamma for refuge," or "They will go to the Saṅgha for refuge," or "I shall satisfy the four assemblies with a great rain of Dhamma." The Blessed Buddhas also wander for another five reasons...
58:
(The Blessed Buddhas) wander with the intention that beings "will abstain from taking life," or "will abstain from taking what is not given... from sexual misconduct... from false speech... from the use of intoxicating drinks and drugs which are the cause of heedlessness."

The Blessed Buddhas also wander for another eight reasons: with the intention that beings "will attain the first jhāna," or "the second jhāna... (and so on) up to the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."

The Blessed Buddhas also wander for another eight reasons: with the intention that beings "will attain the path of stream-entry," or "the fruit of stream-entry... (and so on) up to the realization of the fruit of arahantship."

This is the unhurried wandering (aturita-cārikā), and it is this wandering that is intended here. That unhurried wandering is of two types: fixed wandering (nibaddha-cārikā) and unfixed wandering (anibaddha-cārikā). Among them, wandering for the benefit of a single being capable of awakening is called fixed wandering. Wandering through villages, market towns, and cities in succession is called unfixed wandering. It is this unfixed wandering that is intended here.

"Having set the lodgings in order" (senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā) means storing away the lodgings. In doing so, the Elder did not pack small or large bowls, small or large trays, silk robes, fine cloth robes, and so on; nor did he fill jars with ghee, oil, and such, store them in a room, close the door, and apply keys and seals. Rather, in accordance with the Vinaya instruction: "If there is no monk, novice, monastery attendant, or lay follower, one should place the bed upon four stones, place the chair upon the bed, pile the robes on the robe-pole or robe-rope, close the doors and windows, and then depart," he set them in order merely by informing the resident monk.

"He set out on wandering towards Sāvatthī" means that, desiring to see the Teacher, he departed towards the direction where Sāvatthī was located.
