When he departed, he did so without informing King Suddhodana and without having ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so on taken along. Like a great bull-elephant that has left the herd, or like a lion performing its own task without a companion, he departed alone, taking only his bowl and robes. Why did this Elder not go to Rājagaha with his five hundred disciples but depart only now? Rājagaha is sixty leagues (yojanas) away from Kapilavatthu, while Sāvatthī is only fifteen. The explanation that "he departed upon hearing that the Teacher had traveled forty-five leagues from Rājagaha and was staying in Sāvatthī, and was now nearby" is not a sufficient reason. For one who is going to the presence of the Buddhas would go even a thousand leagues; at that time...
59: However, physical seclusion (kāyaviveka) is difficult to obtain. When traveling with many people, if one says, "Let's go," another says, "Let's stay here." If one says, "Let's stay," another says, "Let's go." Therefore, it is not possible to sit and enter into meditative attainments (samāpatti) at any desired moment, nor is it possible to obtain physical seclusion in a comfortable dwelling. For one who travels alone, however, all of that is easily obtained. Thinking thus, he did not go at that time (in Rājagaha) but set out only now. Regarding the phrase "wandering on tour" (cārikaṃ caramāno): although this wandering on tour for the sake of favoring the masses is obtained only by the Buddhas, by way of traditional usage (ruḷhī) based on the Buddha, it is also used for the disciples. It is like calling a fan made of bamboo strips or such "a palm-leaf fan" (tālavaṇṭa). "Where the Blessed One was" (yena Bhagavā) means: having wandered for alms in a small village not far from Sāvatthī and finished his meal, he entered the Jetavana monastery. Without even having the thought, "I will go to the place of the Elder Sāriputta or the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, wash and rub my feet, drink some water or a beverage, rest for a while, and then see the Teacher," he went directly to the precinct of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi). For the Elder, when he wishes to see the Teacher, there is no need to act through another monk. Therefore, he did not even have the thought, "I will take Rāhula or Ānanda and have them ask for permission before I see the Teacher." The Elder himself was a beloved figure in the Buddha's Dispensation, like a great victorious general of a king. Just as such a general, wishing to see the king, does not need to rely on another's service to see him, but sees him by himself due to being beloved; so too, the Elder was beloved in the Dispensation, and since he had no need to rely on another to see the Teacher, he washed his feet, wiped them with a foot-cloth, and approached where the Blessed One was. The Blessed One also saw, "At dawn, Mantāṇiputta (Venerable Puṇṇa) will arrive." Therefore, having entered the Fragrant Chamber, without even bolting the door (sūcighaṭika), he dispelled his fatigue and sat up. The Elder pushed open the door, entered the Fragrant Chamber, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat at one side. "With a Dhamma talk" (dhammiyā kathāyā) means: when the Blessed One was giving a Dhamma talk, in the Cūḷagosinga Sutta he spoke on the benefits of the harmony of the three clansmen. In the Sekkha Sutta, he spoke on the benefits of the dwelling place; in the Ghaṭikāra Sutta, he spoke on the talk related to past lives (pubbenivāsa) concerning the attainment of mindfulness; in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta...
60:
...in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, he spoke on the four summaries of the Dhamma (dhammuddesa); in the Sela Sutta, he spoke on the benefits of beverages; in the Upakkilesa Sutta, while preaching to the Elder Bhagu, he spoke on the benefits of being alone (ekībhāva). In this Rathavinīta Sutta, however, while preaching to the Venerable Puṇṇa, he showed the infinite methods (anantanaya) based on the ten subjects of talk (dasakathāvatthu), saying, "Puṇṇa, this talk is also talk on fewness of wishes (appicchakathā), it is also talk on contentment (santosakathā)." For a disciple who has reached the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), (such preaching) is like standing on the shore of the great ocean and stretching out one's hand (so easy).

"Towards Andhavana" means: at that time, after the meal, Jetavana was crowded with people. Many people, such as kings and brahmins, frequented Jetavana, making it like a camp for a Wheel-turning King's army, so it was not easy to find seclusion. Andhavana, however, was secluded like a meditation hall. Therefore, Venerable Puṇṇa went towards Andhavana. Why did he not see the Great Elder (Venerable Sāriputta)? It is said he had this thought: "I will come in the evening, see the Great Elder, and then see the Ten-Powered One again. In this way, there will be one attendance on the Great Elders and two on the Teacher. Then, having paid homage to the Teacher, I will go to my own dwelling."

## Sattavisuddhipañhavaṇṇanā

"He was constantly praising" means the Elder Sāriputta lived constantly praising his virtues. It is said that from that day on, every day in the midst of the Saṅgha, the Elder would speak of the virtues of Venerable Puṇṇa to make the senior, middle-seated, and junior monks mindful, saying, "Venerable Puṇṇa, the son of the brahmin lady Mantāṇī, lives unmixed with the four assemblies. He will come to see the Ten-Powered One. I wonder if he will leave without seeing me." The Elder had this thought: "Elderly monks are not always inside the monastery. If his virtues are spoken of, whoever sees that monk will come and inform me." Then, a co-resident (saddhivihārika) of the Elder saw the Venerable Mantāṇiputta taking his bowl and robes and entering the Fragrant Chamber. How did he know it was him? He knew from the Blessed One's Dhamma talk, as He spoke calling "Puṇṇa, Puṇṇa," thinking, "This is the Elder whom my preceptor (upajjhāya) is constantly praising." Thus, he came and informed the Elder. In the phrase "taking the sitting cloth," a sitting cloth (nisīdana) refers to a fringed, non-woven mat. The Elder, however, took a leather mat (cammakhaṇḍa) and went. From behind...
61:
## 
“Piṭṭhito” means following from behind. “Sīsānulokī” means walking while looking at the back [of the person ahead] when on higher ground and looking at the head when on lower ground. He followed in such a manner. Although the Venerable Sāriputta walked very closely, he did not disturb with the sound of his footsteps, as his footsteps were well-restrained. However, knowing that “this is not the time for pleasantries,” he did not stay too close. Since the Andhavana forest is very vast, one might not be seen if hidden in a certain place; fearing that it would be unpleasant to have to call out “Friend Puṇṇa, Friend Puṇṇa,” he walked at a distance, keeping the head in view to know the place where [Puṇṇa] sat. “Divāvihāraṃ nisīdi” means he sat down for the day-abiding (daytime meditation).

In that place, the Venerable Puṇṇa was of noble brahmin birth, and so was the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Puṇṇa was golden-hued, and so was the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Puṇṇa was an attainer of the fruition of Arahatship, and so was the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Puṇṇa had fulfilled perfections for a hundred thousand aeons, while the Venerable Sāriputta had fulfilled perfections for one incalculable and a hundred thousand aeons. The Venerable Puṇṇa was a great Arahant who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and so was the Venerable Sāriputta. Thus, like two lions entering a golden cave, like two tigers descending to their prowling ground, like two Chaddanta elephant kings entering a blooming Sal forest, like two kings of Garudas entering a silk-cotton forest, like two Vessavaṇa deities riding a human-drawn carriage, like two Sakkas sitting on the Paṇḍukambala stone throne, and like two Hārita Mahābrahmas within a single celestial mansion—both of them, being of brahmin birth, golden-hued, attainers of meditative attainments, possessors of fulfilled perfections, and great Arahants with analytical knowledges, entered that forest grove and graced that woodland.

When asked, “Friend, is the holy life lived under the Blessed One?” it means, “Friend, for what purpose is the holy life lived by the venerable one under our Blessed One?” Although the Venerable Sāriputta knew that the Venerable Puṇṇa was living the holy life under the Blessed One, he asked this to initiate a conversation. For a subsequent conversation cannot arise without a preceding one being established; therefore, he asked thus. The Elder, acknowledging it, said, “It is so, friend.” Then, the Venerable Sāriputta, wishing to hear the answer to the question, asked the seven purifications in order, starting with: “Friend, is the holy life lived under the Blessed One for the sake of purification of virtue?” The detailed explanation of these purifications is stated in the Visuddhimagga. The Venerable...
62:
## 
Because the living of the holy life does not reach its summit even if one is established in the fourfold purification of virtue and so forth, the Venerable Puṇṇa rejected them all, saying, “Not so, friend.”

“Friend, if so, for what purpose is it lived?” [Venerable Sāriputta] asked, meaning if the holy life is not lived for the sake of purification of virtue and so forth, then for what purpose is it lived? When he said, “Friend, it is for the sake of Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna),” here “anupādā-parinibbāna” means extinction without conditions (appaccaya-parinibbāna). Clinging (upādāna) is of two kinds: clinging as grasping (gahaṇūpādāna) and clinging as condition (paccayūpādāna). Clinging as grasping refers to the four types of clinging, such as clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna). Clinging as condition refers to the conditions stated as “with ignorance as condition, formations [arise]” (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā).

Among these two, teachers who speak of clinging as grasping explain “anupādā-parinibbāna” as the fruition of Arahatship (arahatta-phala) which occurs without grasping any formation by even one of the four types of clinging. For that [fruition] does not grasp any state by being associated with clinging, and it is called “parinibbāna” because it arises at the extinction of defilements. However, teachers who speak of clinging as condition explain “anupādā-parinibbāna” as extinction without conditions (appaccaya-parinibbāna). They explain only the unconditioned state (asaṅkhata-dhamma), the deathless element (amata-dhātu), which does not arise by way of conditions, as “anupādā-parinibbāna.” This is the end, this is the summit, this is the conclusion. For one who has reached Nibbāna without conditions, the living of the holy life is said to have reached its summit; therefore, the Elder said, “For the sake of Nibbāna without clinging.” Then, the Venerable Sāriputta, wishing to cross-examine him, began to ask again: “Friend, is purification of virtue Nibbāna without clinging?”

The Elder also rejected it in the same way in all turns, and finally, wishing to show the fault, said, “Friend, if purification of virtue [were Nibbāna without clinging]...” and so forth. In that statement, “paññapeyya” means “if one were to designate.” To designate a state that is with clinging as Nibbāna without clinging means that one would be designating a state that is to be grasped as a state not to be grasped, a state with conditions as a state without conditions, and a conditioned state as an unconditioned state. In the case of purification by knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana-visuddhi), this same meaning should be taken: that one would be designating a state with conditions as a state without conditions, and a conditioned state as an unconditioned state. In the phrase “Friend, a worldling,” one should understand the mundane foolish worldling (bālaputhujjana) who follows the round of rebirths. Since that worldling lacks even the mere fourfold purification of virtue, he is entirely apart from these states. “If so” means “for the reason that some wise people understand the meaning through a simile, for that reason I shall give you a simile.”
63: ## Commentary on the Sattarathavinīta Sutta "Satta rathavinītāni" refers to seven chariots drawn by well-trained thoroughbred horses. In the phrase, "Friend, this purification of virtue is only for the sake of purification of mind," the word "cittavisuddhatthā" is in the ablative case (nissakkavacana). The meaning here is: as long as there is the benefit known as purification of mind, this purification of virtue is desired. Whatever purification of mind exists, that is the benefit of purification of virtue; it is the pinnacle, it is the end. This is because for one established in purification of mind, the task of purification of virtue is said to be completed. This method should be understood for all terms. In this context, the comparison with the simile is as follows: The practitioner (yogāvacara) who is afraid of aging and death should be regarded like King Pasenadi of Kosala. The city of identity (sakkāya) is like the city of Sāvatthī, and the great city of Nibbāna is like the city of Sāketa. The time when an urgent matter arises for the king, which brings prosperity in the city of Sāketa and must be reached quickly, should be regarded as the time when the task of realizing the four Noble Truths, not yet understood, arises for the yogi. The seven purifications should be regarded like the seven relay chariots. The time of being established in the purification of virtue is like the time of mounting the first relay chariot. The time of being established in the purification of mind and so on, by means of the purification of virtue and so on, is like the time of mounting the second chariot and so on, by means of the first relay chariot and so on. Just as when one reaches the gate of the inner palace in Sāketa by the seventh relay chariot, descends, and enjoys excellent food on the palace terrace surrounded by a group of relatives and friends, so too should be regarded the time when the yogi, having exhausted all defilements through the purification by knowledge and vision, ascends the noble palace of Dhamma, enters the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) taking Nibbāna as the object, surrounded by the fifty-six wholesome states, and experiences supramundane bliss while dwelling in the couch of cessation (nirodhasayana). Thus, the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, questioned the Venerable Puṇṇa, who possessed the ten subjects of talk, about the seven purifications. The Venerable Puṇṇa answered regarding the ten subjects of talk. In this questioning, did the General of the Dhamma ask knowing or not knowing? Did he ask as an expert (titthakusala) in his own field, or as one who is not an expert in a field not his own? And did the Venerable Puṇṇa answer knowing or not knowing? Did he answer as an expert in his own field, or as one who is not an expert in a field not his own? If one says he asked knowing and as an expert in his own field, it refers only to the General of the Dhamma. If one says he answered knowing and as an expert in his own field...
64: ...it refers only to the Elder Puṇṇa. For what is concise in the purifications is detailed in the subjects of talk. What is concise in the subjects of talk is detailed in the purifications. This should be understood by this method. Among the purifications, the single purification of virtue appears as four subjects of talk: talk on fewness of wishes (appicchakathā), talk on contentment (santuṭṭhikathā), talk on seclusion (asaṃsaggakathā), and talk on virtue (sīlakathā). The single purification of mind appears as three subjects of talk: talk on solitude (pavivekakathā), talk on arousal of energy (vīriyārambhakathā), and talk on concentration (samādhikathā). Thus, first, what is concise in the purifications is detailed in the subjects of talk. Among the subjects of talk, however, the single talk on wisdom (paññākathā) appears as five purifications: purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi), purification by overcoming doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi), purification by knowledge and vision of what is and what is not the path (maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi), purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi), and purification by knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassanavisuddhi). Thus, what is concise in the subjects of talk is detailed in the purifications. Therefore, although the Elder Sāriputta asked about the seven purifications, he did not ask about anything else; he asked only about the ten subjects of talk. The Elder Puṇṇa, too, although answering about the seven purifications, did not answer about anything else; he answered only about the ten subjects of talk. Thus, it should be understood that both these Elders, being knowledgeable and experts in their fields, asked and answered questions only within their own domain. In asking "What is the Venerable's name?", the Elder did not not know his name. He asked even though he knew, in order to have the opportunity to converse joyfully. The phrase "How is the Venerable?" was said by the Elder as a pleasant greeting. "Mantāṇiputta" means the son of the Brahmin lady Mantāṇī. In the phrase "yathā taṃ", "taṃ" is merely a particle, and the concise meaning is "just as a learned disciple should answer, so it was answered." "Anumassa anumassa" means repeatedly reflecting upon and penetrating the ten subjects of talk. In the word "celaṇḍupakena", "cela" refers to cloth and "aṇḍupaka" refers to a coil (pad). By placing a cloth-coil on their heads and seating the Venerable upon it to carry him, fellow practitioners would get the chance to see him; and such a sight would be for their benefit. Thus, by imagining an impossible situation (aṭṭhānaparikappa), he showed a means for frequent viewing. One who cannot carry him in this way, but wishes to ask a question or hear the Dhamma, must go about searching, "Where is the Elder staying? Where is he sitting?" But those who carry him in this way can, at any desired moment, lower him from their heads, seat him on a costly seat, and be able to ask questions or hear the Dhamma. Thus, by imagining an impossible situation, he showed a means for frequent viewing. "Sāriputta" means "fellow practitioners know me as the son of the Brahmin lady Sārī." "Satthukappena" means an Elder who is like the Teacher (the Buddha). Thus, with a single word...
65:
Venerable Puṇṇa extolled Venerable Sāriputta as if placing him against the orb of the moon. Indeed, in this context, the Elder's status as a pre-eminent Dhamma preacher (dhammakathika) became evident. One who wishes to call a minister or a royal chaplain 'great' might say he is like a king. One might say an ox is the size of an elephant, a lake the size of an ocean, or a light the size of the light of the sun and moon. Beyond these measures, there is no further talk of their greatness. Similarly, one who wishes to call a disciple 'great' might say he is like the Teacher (the Buddha). Beyond saying he is like the Buddha, there is no further talk of that disciple's greatness. Thus, with a single statement, Venerable Puṇṇa extolled the Elder as if placing him against the orb of the moon.

Regarding the phrase "May this not be apparent even to us," for one who has attained the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), there is no such thing as lack of clarity (non-manifestation of knowledge). However, one should not take this simile literally but rather speak of its meaning. The reason is that similes are brought in for those who do not understand; this is the intention here. But in the Commentary, this point is rejected, stating that similes are brought in even in the presence of the Buddhas; Venerable Puṇṇa said this out of respect for the Elder.

"Anumassa anumassa pucchitā" means questioning by repeatedly delving into the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu). Is asking a question difficult, or is answering it difficult? Asking after learning and memorizing is not very difficult, but answering is difficult. Both asking and answering with reasons and causes are indeed difficult. "Samanumodisu" means they rejoiced with a common mind. Thus, the teaching is concluded according to the sequence of connections.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Rathavinīta Sutta is finished.
## 5. Explanation of the Nivāpa Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Nivāpa Sutta. In that sutta, "nevāpika" refers to one who sows grass seeds in the forest to catch deer. He thinks, "I will easily catch the deer that come to eat this grass." "Nivāpa" means the sowing (the bait). "Nivutta" means that which is sown. "Migajāta" means a herd of deer. "Anupakhajja" means having entered into. "Mucchitā" means infatuated with the infatuation of craving; it is the state of infatuation where craving enters the heart.
66:
It means "having been brought to" (pāpitā). "They will fall into intoxication" means they will fall into the intoxication of conceit (māna). "Negligence" (pamāda) refers to the state of being devoid of mindfulness. "They will become such as can be dealt with as desired" means they will become those who must act according to our (the hunters') will. "In this sown area" means in this place where grass is sown. It is said that there is a certain sown grass field called "Nidāghabhaddaka" which is good in the summer. As the summer progresses, that field becomes dense and thick like a thicket of nīvāra or like a mass of rain clouds. Hunters plow and sow that grass in a place where water is easily available, fence it in, install a gate, and guard it. Then, in the height of summer when all other grasses are dry and even enough water to wet the tongue is hard to find, the deer wander about trembling while eating dry grass and old leaves. When they catch the scent of that sown grass, they no longer care about being killed or bound; they leap over the fence and enter. This is because that sown grass is extremely dear and pleasing to those deer. Even when the hunter sees those deer, he acts as if he is negligent for two or three days and leaves the gate open. Inside the sown area, there are also water holes in various places. The deer enter through the open gate, merely eat and drink, and then leave. The next day, thinking "They aren't doing anything to us," they eat and drink while shaking their ears and go about leisurely. The day after that, thinking "There is no one to do anything," they eat and drink as much as they want, then enter a thicket and lie down. When the hunters know the deer are negligent, they close the gate, surround them, and starting from one side, they strike and kill them. In this way, those deer in that sown area become such as can be dealt with according to the hunter's will.

"Monks, among those deer" means among that herd of deer. "The first herd of deer"—although there are no specific names like first or second, the Blessed One assigned names like first, second, third, and fourth to show them in the order they occurred. "Power and majesty" (iddhānubhāva) is due to the ability to act as one desires. Here, "iddhi" and "ānubhāva" refer to mastery (vasībhāva), the ability to make things happen according to one's will.

"Eating with fear" means eating while being afraid of danger. "Strength and energy" refers to the air element (vāyodhātu) that moves back and forth; the meaning is that this element declines.

"We shall make our dwelling nearby" means they thought: "There is danger if we sleep and eat inside, and there is danger if we come from outside to eat. Let us make our dwelling in a place nearby, depending on this sown area."
67:
'They made their dwelling nearby' means that hunters cannot remain vigilant at all times. Thinking, 'We will sleep in various thickets and at the foot of fences, and when those hunters depart to wash their faces or to eat, we will enter the meadow (nivāpa), eat just enough, and return to our dwelling,' they made their dwelling in thickets, at the foot of fences, and so forth, relying on the meadow.

'They ate' means that, knowing the time of the hunters' negligence in the manner described, they entered quickly and ate. 'Deceptive ones' means those with trained craftiness. 'Powerful ones' means as if they were powerful. 'Other people' means yakkhas (demons). These are not of the deer species.

'Either coming or going' means 'we do not know their coming or going, such as from which place they come or to which place they go.' 'With nets supported by sticks' means with nets held up by poles. 'They surrounded the area on all sides' means thinking, 'These deer are very deceptive; they will not go far, they will be sleeping nearby,' they surrounded and blocked a large area around the meadow. 'They saw' means that after surrounding it, they saw them when they shook the nets all around and looked. 'Where those' means the place where those deer were caught; the meaning is that they saw that place.

'Perhaps we [should stay] where they cannot reach' means those deer thought: 'There is danger for those who sleep and eat inside the meadow, there is danger for those who come from outside to eat, and there is danger for those who live and eat nearby. They too are caught by being surrounded with nets.' Therefore, the thought occurred to them: 'What if we were to make our beds in places where the hunter and his followers cannot reach, which is beyond their range?'

'Others will disturb them' means other people living further away from various places will disturb them. 'Those others who are disturbed' means those others who are disturbed will, in turn, disturb those living even further away. 'In this way, all the deer will completely abandon this bait (meadow) we have laid' means in this way, all the herds of deer, the groups of deer, will give up and abandon this bait laid by us.

'Let us be indifferent' means 'let us remain without effort to catch them.' For when they come as they please, it is easy to catch a young fawn, an old deer, a weak deer, or one separated from the herd; but if they do not come, nothing can be obtained. 'Monks, they were indifferent' means that having thought thus, they remained without making an effort to catch them.
68:
In the phrase "this pasture (nivāpa) sown by Māra, and these worldly baits (lokāmisa)," the names "pasture" and "worldly baits" are designations for the five cords of sensual pleasure, which are the baits of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭāmisa). Māra does not wander about sowing sensual pleasures like one sows seeds; however, he exerts his influence over those who are greedy for sensual pleasures. Therefore, sensual pleasures are called the pasture (nivāpa) sown by Māra. Thus it is said: "this pasture sown by Māra." "They did not escape from the power of Māra’s influence" means they came under Māra’s control and became subject to his will. This is the metaphor that comes in the context of renunciation along with wife and children.

"Clear deliverance of mind (ceto-vimutti) declines"—here, "clear deliverance of mind" refers to the intention (ajjhāsaya) that arises thinking, "I will live in the forest." The meaning is that this intention declines. "I speak of these second persons who are like that metaphor"—this is the metaphor for the "Brahmin-righteous renunciation" (brāhmaṇadhammika-pabbajjā). Indeed, Brahmins practice the holy life in celibacy for forty-eight years, and then, fearing the interruption of the round of rebirth, they think, "We shall continue the lineage," seek wealth, take a wife, and live in the midst of a household. When a son is born, they say, "A son is born to us; the round is not interrupted; the lineage is continued," and they go forth to renounce again, or they continue to live with that same wife.

Monks, in this way, those third recluses and brahmins also did not escape; like the previous persons, they did not escape from the power of Māra’s influence and remained subject to his will. What did they do? They descended into villages, market towns, and royal capitals, and living there in hermitages built in various parks and gardens, they taught the sons of good families various arts such as the art of elephants, horses, and chariots. Thus, like the third group of deer caught in a stake-supported net, they were surrounded by the net of wrong views (diṭṭhijāla) of the Evil Māra and became subject to his will.

"I speak of these fourth persons who are like that metaphor"—this is a statement brought as a metaphor for this Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Buddha.

"He made Māra blind" does not mean he gouged out Māra’s eyes. Rather, Māra is unable to see the mind of a monk who has attained a Jhana that serves as a basis for Insight (vipassanā-pādaka-jhāna), thinking, "The mind is occurring depending on such-and-such an object." Therefore, it is said: "He made Māra blind." "Having obliterated Māra’s vision so it is trackless" means, by that same method, the eye of Māra...
69:
When this is done, it means that the eye of Māra becomes without a footing, without an object, without a foundation, and devoid of an objective support. 'Gone beyond the sight of the Evil One' means that by that very method, he has gone beyond the sight of Māra, the Evil One. Indeed, that Evil One is unable to see with his fleshly eye the knowledge-body (ñāṇasarīra) of that monk who has attained the jhāna which is the basis for insight (vipassanā). 'Having seen with wisdom, the taints are exhausted' means that having seen the Four Noble Truths with the wisdom of the Path, the four taints are completely exhausted.

'One who has crossed over the craving (visattikā) in the world' refers to craving, which is called 'visattikā' because it has the nature of clinging to beings in the world. Alternatively, why is it called 'visattikā'? It is called 'visattikā' because it spreads (visata), because it is abundant (vipula), because it is extensive (visāla), because it is uneven (visama), because it clings (visakkati), because it carries poison (visaṃ harati), because it is deceptive (visamvādikā), because it has poison as its root (visamūlā), because it has poison as its fruit (visaphalā), and because it is like the consumption of poison (visaparibhogā). That craving spreads extensively in the objects of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. Thus, one has crossed over, transcended, and surmounted the craving called 'visattikā'. Therefore, it is said: 'One who has crossed over the craving in the world.'

## The Commentary on the Nivāpa Sutta
## in the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary named Papañcasūdanī is finished.
## 6. Commentary on the Pāsarāsi Sutta

'Thus have I heard' and so forth is the Pāsarāsi Sutta. In that sutta, they speak by way of requesting, 'It is well, friends.' It is heard that these five hundred monks living in the countryside arrived at Sāvatthī thinking, 'We shall see the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala).' Although they obtained the sight of the Teacher, they had not yet heard a Dhamma talk. Out of reverence for the Teacher, they did not dare to say, 'Venerable Sir, please give us a Dhamma talk.' For the Buddhas are majestic, difficult to approach and awe-inspiring, like a lion, the king of beasts, wandering alone in the forest; like a noble tusker elephant; like a great cobra with its hood raised; and like a great mass of fire. Regarding this, it is also said:

'Like a terrifying cobra,
Like a lion, the king of beasts,
Like a noble tusker elephant,
Thus the Buddhas are difficult to approach.'
